articles.title: Black Sea sailors thought a rescue boat was racing toward them. Instead, it was a drone that sank their ship
articles.summary: The Dignity is one of nearly 50 commercial vessels that maritime analysts say have been attacked in the Black Sea in October alone. The strikes are part of an escalating conflict that has brought…

image.caption: Ashraf Mamdouh, a rescued seafarer from the HS Dignity, sits in a hotel room in Varna, Bulgaria. He is one of five crew members who were rescued after the ship sank. He and the others are not allowed to leave the hotel while they wait for new identification documents that will allow them to travel h

blocks.text: In the early hours of Oct. 13, the crew from the HS Dignity gathered on the deck of the cargo ship and put on life jackets as the vessel rocked in the churning waves of the Black Sea. The captain had given the order to abandon the vessel because it was sinking after a sea drone struck its hull.

As the 16-man crew, made up of Syrian and Egyptian nationals, peered into the darkness, they spotted the outline of a boat moving quickly toward them. They shone their flashlights, thinking rescuers might have already responded to their distress call.
But what they saw alarmed them.
No one was driving the boat.
“We realized that this boat was also part of the group that was attacking us. Of course, we all ran,” said Ashraf Mamdouh, the vessel's 42-year-old chief officer.
The sea drone rammed directly into the ship.
“The vessel began sinking rapidly into the water. The whole crew was falling to the deck; nobody could stand properly because of the impact and the chaos,” he said.
“We didn't have time to finish launching the lifeboats.”
Inside dramatic rescue as drones hit hundreds of ships in Black Sea
The Dignity is one of nearly 50 commercial vessels that maritime analysts say have been attacked in the Black Sea this month as the conflict between Russia and Ukraine escalates at sea.
The strikes have brought much of the traffic through the key shipping corridor to a halt and prompted NATO to step up maritime security, including by deploying more patrol boats and radar.
More than 30 killed or missing
At least 31 seafarers have been killed or are missing in the attacks.
Many of the vessels that were recently attacked were travelling through the western Black Sea, including some that were struck off the coasts of NATO members Bulgaria and Romania.

On Friday, a search-and-rescue operation was underway after a ship flagged to Comoros, a small archipelago off the coast of East Africa, was struck by drones just outside Romania's territorial waters.
The crew of 13 included Ukrainian and Azerbaijani sailors. One body has been recovered, while officials say three people remain missing.
Romanian President Nicușor Dan blamed Russia for the attacks.

Data shared with CBC News by maritime risk management firm Ambrey suggest there have been more than 500 attacks on commercial vessels this year in the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov, which are connected by the narrow Kerch Strait.
Of the 45 attacks recorded in October, Ambrey believes Russia was responsible for 40.
Russia's Ministry of Defence has acknowledged striking dozens of ships this month alone in social media posts, almost always claiming the vessels were supporting Ukraine's military.
But Mamdouh, who spoke to CBC News from a hotel in Varna, Bulgaria, said the Dignity had sailed from Algeria and was headed for Romania, where it was scheduled to pick up grain.
Ashraf Mamdouh, the chief officer aboard the HS Dignity, arrives in Varna, Bulgaria, on Oct. 13 after his ship sank when it was hit by two sea drones. (Nikolay Doychinov/AFP/Getty Images)
Adrift in the Black Sea
The Dignity had already been at sea for more than a month when the drones struck at about 1:30 a.m.
Mamdouh and other experienced crew members urged everyone aboard to get as far away from the ship as possible to avoid being pulled under as the 123-metre vessel sank beneath the churning waves.

“We tried to gather together to reduce everyone's fear and panic. We wanted to remain in one group so that, if a rescue team arrived, it would be easier for them to rescue as many people as possible,” Mamdouh said.
This undated image of the HS Dignity shows the ship before it sank in the Black Sea on Oct. 13. (Submitted by Ashraf Mamdouh)
He began calling out to other crew members, but the strong winds drowned out their voices.
“I started asking everyone, ‘Why are you moving away from each other?’ I hadn't realized that I was drifting away, too. The sea currents were separating us.”
At one point, a life raft suddenly appeared beside him. He climbed aboard and lay there for four hours, until another commercial vessel appeared nearby.
Still clutching his cellphone, he switched on its flashlight to attract the attention of the crew aboard the Azov Concord.
Cargo ships are seen in the Black Sea from Port Varna, in Varna, eastern Bulgaria on October 13. (Nikolay Doychinov/AFP/Getty Images)
18-year-old among the missing

Mamdouh was pulled from the water and is one of five crew members who survived. Eleven remain officially listed as missing, including 18-year-old Hamza Suleiman, a Syrian who was on his first voyage aboard a ship.
“The last phone call between Hamza and me was on the night of Oct. 12,” said his father, Basel, who spoke to CBC News via Zoom from Tartus, Syria.
“Hamza contacted us and said hi to his mother and reassured us. He said, ‘Dad, we're in Bulgaria now.’”
Basel said his son had taken the job aboard the Syrian-owned ship because he expected to work in the engine room, where he hoped to learn more about engineering.
Hamza Suleiman, 18, boarded the HS Dignity in August for his first job as a seafarer. He has been missing since the vessel sank on Oct. 13 off the coast of Bulgaria. (Submitted by Basel Suleiman)
But he became disillusioned when he was assigned to work on the deck. He grew increasingly fearful after learning that another vessel, the Alfa Watan, had been struck by drones on Oct. 6.
Ten crew members aboard that ship, most of them Syrian, have yet to be recovered.
After the Alfa Watan attack, Suleiman spoke with his son, who said he wanted to leave the vessel.
Basel Suleiman told CBC News he tried contacting the ship's owners to arrange for his son to disembark in Turkey, but the young man remained aboard.

Mamdouh, who spoke with Suleiman's father, told him that the last time he saw his son, the young man was aboard the ship wearing a life jacket. That detail has helped sustain his father's hope that he might still be alive.
Basel agreed to speak publicly about his son despite the uncertainty surrounding his fate.
“We don't have the ability to reach the [Bulgarian] authorities or to go and look for our children with our own hands,” he said.

Khaldoun Nabelsi, head of the Syrian Seafarers Association of the U.K., said he had been in contact with several families whose relatives had been killed in strikes on commercial vessels. He said he had counted at least 18 Syrian seafarers killed.
“Nobody is forced to take these jobs, but in other ways you are forced. If you want to work, you have to go,” Nabelsi said.
“They have to find a deal to stop this. But from our side, as a seaman or as a shipping company, we can do nothing.”
The deteriorating security situation has prompted the Philippine government to issue a directive prohibiting its citizens from boarding vessels navigating the northern stretches of the Black Sea.

In an image supplied by the Romanian government, the fire-damaged Royad Mammadov ship sits in the Black Sea on Oct. 5 after a suspected drone strike that killed two people. (Romanian Interior Ministry/Handout/Reuters)
Shipping companies scale back operations
Some shipping companies that normally operate in the region are avoiding it altogether or have sharply reduced the number of vessels they deploy there.

Turkey-based ED Shipping has a fleet of 26 vessels, but 19 are currently “laid up,” meaning they are temporarily out of service and not operating at sea, said the company's chief financial officer, Demre İşcen.
One of the company's ships, the Circon, was struck on June 5 while transiting the Sea of Azov. Two crew members were killed.

Ukraine carried out the attack, acknowledging that it had targeted five vessels that night, including ships stationed at occupied Ukrainian ports. Ukraine said the vessels were involved in transporting stolen Ukrainian grain, as well as military cargo and fuel.
İşcen disputes that account, saying the Circon was on its way to a port in the Sea of Azov near Rostov-on-Don, Russia, where he said the company had a contract to load Russian grain.

“Our crew members are Azeri and Turkish nationals. We didn't have anything to do with Ukraine. We didn't have anything to do with occupied-area grain … stolen grain, whatever,” he told CBC News in an interview from Istanbul.

“Ninety per cent of the time, we carry grain cargo from Russia to Turkey, Bulgaria, Romania, Moldova, Georgia, Greece, all around the Mediterranean, Aegean Sea, Red Sea, Black Sea. This is our main trading area.”
İşcen said the company was losing millions of dollars every month and that some of its seafarers were out of work because its ships were no longer travelling to Black Sea ports.
Other mariners say they will refuse any work in the region.
Mamdouh remains in Bulgaria with the other surviving members of the Dignity's crew. They are waiting for new documents so they can leave Europe and fly home.
“I will not go back to the Black Sea again. Never,” he said.
“This situation is too dangerous.”
A Bulgarian border police vessel carrying crew members from a ship damaged in a drone attack, in Varna, Bulgaria, on Oct. 6. (Petko Momchilov/Reuters)

articles.title: Why a new round in the U.S.-Iran conflict could be the most devastating yet
articles.summary: As the U.S. midterm elections approach, intelligence analysts warn that the United States and Israel are preparing for a devastating third round of direct military conflict with Iran. Experts caution…

image.caption: Iranian missiles are displayed next to a banner with a picture of Iranain Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, on a street in Tehran on Sept. 27. (Majid Asgaripour/West Asia News Agency via REUTERS)

blocks.text: The warning signs are flashing red with indications that once the ballots are counted in the U.S. midterm elections, the United States and Israel will relaunch their war with Iran.
The next round of attacks could be more devastating than the first, warn analysts.

"A renewed war seems almost inevitable," said Danny Citrinowicz, an Israeli Middle East and Iran analyst whose earlier warnings and cautions about the risks of a direct conflict with Iran were largely borne out by events.

Citrinowicz, who worked for Israel's military as an intelligence official for more than two decades, had initially warned that any U.S. and Israeli attack on the Islamic regime would not likely lead to regime change but would instead end up engulfing the entire region in a wider conflict — an assessment that proved true.
In an interview with CBC News, he said that assessment still holds.
"The problem is there is no silver bullet solution to the impasse we are now at in the Persian Gulf and in front of Trump he has only bad and worse options."

Under U.S. President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, their countries broke with decades of restraint and shadow warfare and launched two distinct wars with Iran over the past 18 months.
Iranian women look at a building, which was damaged in a U.S. and Israeli strike in March, in Tehran on Aug. 22. (Reuters)
The first in June 2025 began with U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities, lasted 12 days and ended with a fragile ceasefire.

The conflict roared back to life in February of this year following a massive U.S. military buildup in the region. It began with Israel's strikes against Iran's senior leadership, including Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
Worst round yet
Citrinowicz, who's with Israel's Institute for National Security Studies, said a third round of war could be the worst yet, based on what Iranian officials are telegraphing.

"They will attack the energy facilities in the Gulf. But more than that, they will cause significant damage to civilian infrastructure, communications, as well as cutting off the internet lines going under [the] Hormuz Strait," he said.
He said there is even a possibility that Iran could push some of its massive land army into the fight with limited assaults against Gulf countries that house U.S. bases, such as Kuwait and Bahrain.
"We'll see a regional war with Iran investing a lot in attacking the U.S. presence in the region to cause maximum economical damage to the U.S. international economy."

Smoke rises from a burning vessel, following what the U.S. Central Command said was a strike on an Iranian-affiliated dhow, at a location given as the Gulf of Oman, in this still image taken from a video released on Oct. 14. (U.S. Central Command/Reuters)
Midterm dynamics

While both sides have largely avoided fresh strikes against each other's bases or territory since the summer truce collapsed, the conflict remains active. The U.S. imposed a naval blockade of Iranian ports and Iran has continued to target commercial shipping traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, driving up global energy costs.

Posting on Truth Social Thursday, Trump blamed Iran for trying to artificially drive up oil prices ahead of the midterms on Nov. 3, elections that many pollsters believe will see Trump's Republicans lose control of the House of Representatives and possibly the Senate as well.
"They are even making up fake hits, mines and everything else," said Trump, implying that Iran is exaggerating the extent of the damage it's causing.

A report published this week by the Washington, D.C.,-based Critical Threats Project alongside the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) also suggested Iran is trying to use strikes on shipping to weaken Trump's position heading into the elections.

"The increase in Iranian attacks on vessels is part of the ongoing Iranian campaign to pressure the United States to meet Iranian demands, including control over the Strait, by driving up global prices," the report said.
People walk on the beach, with vessels in the Strait of Hormuz visible near the beach of Bandar Abbas, Iran, on Oct. 13. (Razieh Poudat West Asia News Agency/Reuters)
Iran's demands

Iran's government wants relief from punishing sanctions, reparations for the damage caused by earlier U.S.-Israel strikes, the release of billions of dollars in frozen Iranian assets and the right to keep its supplies of enriched uranium.
Mediators with Pakistan and Qatar have spent weeks trying to push diplomatic solutions to get the two sides talking again, but to no avail.
For both Netanyahu and Trump, the war with Iran remains unfinished business.

items: Iran says 7 ships have been struck in Strait of Hormuz, Saudis intercept drones in airspace
Iran's president says country won't surrender after Trump threat to 'annihilate' Islamic republic

blocks.text: The Islamic regime not only remains in power, but its leadership has also proven remarkably adept at adapting to both the military strikes and the economic blockade imposed by the West.

"The war in some respects has probably persuaded Iran's leadership to double down on their commitment to the revolutionary ideology that has really forged this regime," said Suzanne Maloney, a vice-president and director of the foreign policy program at the Washington, D.C.,-based Brookings Institution.
Like Citroniwicz, she said if war resumes, Trump won't be able to easily contain it.
"The retaliation as we've seen will come not just from Iran, but from its proxies and partners in the region," she said, referring to the Houthi militias in Yemen and Hezbollah in Lebanon.
Iran's goal won't just be to hit back at U.S. military targets but also soft economic targets, such as airports, that could undermine Gulf countries for years to come, she said.
How the Houthi-Saudi Arabia conflict plays into broader Middle East war
Maloney and Karim Sadjadpour, a prominent Iran expert with the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, were speaking on an online Carnegie panel about the future of the war in Iran.
"I genuinely don't think that President Trump has a clear idea in his head what he's trying to achieve," said Sadjadpour.
"I don't see any possibility of what Trump is looking for — which is like a knockout punch, a military strike — which will essentially force the Iranians into a compromise or capitulation."
Nuclear timeline?
Trump claimed his justification for the initial attacks on Iran was to ensure the country doesn't get a nuclear weapon.

At the time, while Iran possessed enough enriched uranium to theoretically pursue a weapon, many independent experts and U.S. intelligence sources believed it was still likely months away from doing so — and perhaps more importantly, that the regime's supreme leader had not yet made the definitive political decision to cross the nuclear threshold.
Since those initial June 2025 strikes, the human cost of the war has been severe.
Western NGOs claim the death toll in Iran is well over 7,000, including civilians and government figures who have been killed in the joint U.S.-Israeli strikes.
Lebanon has also suffered an especially heavy toll, with local media reporting more than 4,000 fatalities.
Twenty-one U.S. service members were killed, mostly by Iranian strikes on U.S. bases in the Persian Gulf, while more than 70 Israelis have died.
People drive near a billboard depicting U.S. President Donald Trump on a building in Tehran on Sept. 16. (Majid Asgaripour/WANA/Reuters)
There have also been deaths throughout the Gulf countries, including the UAE and Saudi Arabia, as well as in Iraq and Yemen.
The New York Times and other U.S. media are reporting the Pentagon is working on a new battle plan for the possible next round of attacks — but whether Trump will ultimately authorize it is unknown.
'Finishing the job'
Israel's leadership, on the other hand, has made no secret of its push to restart the conflict, with Netanyahu explicitly stating his desire to bring down the Iran regime by "finishing the job."
Netanyahu faces Israeli voters in the coming days, and whether he hangs onto his job could end up in a photo finish.

items: Netanyahu faces fresh allegations he ignored warnings about Oct. 7 — right before an election

blocks.text: Relaunching the war with Iran could offer him a tactical way to stay in power; even if his party loses seats, a widening security crisis could lead to the creation of an emergency unity government with members of the opposition, said Citrinowicz.

"The real risk is that Netanyahu will involve his political considerations together with some other operational development in Iran that he is going to not necessarily invent, but probably [inflate]," he said.
A shopkeeper works at his shop in a local market in Tehran on Sept. 26. (Majid Asgaripour/West Asia News Agency/Reuters)
"And this combination will lead to an unnecessary attack against Iran."
Sadjadpour from the Carnegie panel said there is no obvious military way out of the impasse and says Trump's maximalist goals have closed down diplomatic options as well.

"I believe there's a pretty clear formula under which it [Iran's government] compromises," said Sadjadpour. "It's when it faces what I would describe as existential economic pressure, coupled with a clear, limited diplomatic exit.
"If you're asking them to change their identity, that's not going to succeed."

articles.summary: The warrant of arrest is issued by Branch 10 of the Davao City Regional Trial Court, Meanwhile, Lustre says he does not know who the complainant is.

blocks.text: PHILIP LUSTRE. Veteran journalist and author Philip Lustre Jr. is arrested for alleged cyberlibel.
Philip Lustre Jr's Facebook
The warrant of arrest is issued by Branch 10 of the Davao City Regional Trial Court, Meanwhile, Lustre says he does not know who the complainant is.

MANILA, Philippines – Veteran journalist Philip Lustre Jr. was arrested by the Quezon City Police Department (QCPD) under the leadership of acting district director Police Brigadier General (PBGEN) Christopher Olazo on Saturday, October 24, for alleged cyber libel.
The Kamuning Police Station 10’s warrant section and the Quezon City District’s anti-cybercrime team both facilitated the arrest.
Lustre, 72, is the author behind Kill, Kill, Kill: Extrajudicial Killings in the Philippines, a book about former president Rodrigo Duterte’s deadly war on drugs.

He had been attending the House of Representatives’ Saturday news forum at a restaurant along Scout Borromeo Street when the police arrived to read his Miranda rights to him, according to a report by GMA News.
The same report also said lawyer Dino De Leon, who was also present at the forum, will serve as Lustre’s legal counsel moving forward.
Notably, the warrant of arrest was issued by Branch 10 of Davao City’s Regional Trial Court.

Lustre’s arrest comes just after Davao City 1st District Representative Paolo “Pulong” Duterte filed a cyber libel complaint against GMA Network’s journalists over a report about bribery claims against him and Vice President Sara Duterte.

blocks.text: In a video posted by ABS-CBN News, Lustre said he does not know who the complainant is.

articles.title: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un arrives in Chinese border city
articles.summary: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un has reportedly arrived in the Chinese border city of Dandong via a newly opened bridge linking the two countries, South Korea's Yonhap news agency said.

image.caption: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un arrived in China via the newly opened bridge. Image: Florence Lo/REUTERS

blocks.text: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un arrived in China via the newly opened bridge, South Korea’s Yonhap news agency reported on Saturday.
"It appears that Kim Jong Un has arrived in Dandong, China, via the New Yalu River Bridge," the unnamed source said.
The four-lane bridge was completed in 2014 but remained unused for 12 years due to a lack of connecting roads and customs facilities on the North Korean side.
It officially opened about a week ago, marking a step towards strengthening economic ties between the neighbouring countries.

China is North Korea’s largest trading partner and a key source of diplomatic, economic and political support for the isolated, nuclear-armed state, though relations between the two have not always been smooth.
Bridge highlights North Korea's ties with China
The New Yalu River Bridge opened just over a month after North Korea and Russia inaugurated their first road bridge, which Pyongyang hailed as a sign of closer ties.
While North Korea’s trade with Russia largely involves military supplies, trade with China could provide goods needed to develop its civilian economy, analysts say.

articles.title: De Lima, Paolo Duterte clash over libel complaints vs media
articles.summary: Rep. Leila de Lima said Paolo Duterte's libel and cyber libel complaints against GMA Network send a "chilling" message to journalists.

blocks.text: October 24, 2026 | 3:26pm
Composte image shows Rep. Paolo Duterte (Davao City) as photographed in July 2025 and Rep. Leila de Lima (ML Party-list) in September 2026.
Duterte office; De Lima office; Philstar.com composite
MANILA, Philippines — Rep. Leila de Lima (ML Party-list) said Rep. Paolo Duterte's libel and cyber libel complaints against GMA Network send a "chilling" message to journalists.
De Lima criticized Duterte's complaints in a social media post Friday, October 23, saying journalists should not face punishment for reporting allegations of corruption.
"Filing a libel case against a media network and its journalists for doing their job of reporting allegations of corruption sends a chilling message to other media practitioners," De Lima said.
She said attacks against GMA Network and other media outlets following the filing could also be read as a warning to journalists that they "could be the next to be sued."
"This is clearly an attempt to silence journalists and truth-seekers, depriving them of their freedom of the press," De Lima said.

She linked the complaints to what she described as the Duterte family's history of conflict with media organizations, citing actions involving Rappler, the Philippine Daily Inquirer and ABS-CBN during the administration of former President Rodrigo Duterte.
De Lima said journalists merely reported accusations made by witnesses and argued that seeking information about the allegations was part of their responsibility to the public.

The lawmaker, a former human rights commissioner and justice secretary, had led investigations into killings in Davao City. She was later detained on drug-related charges during Rodrigo Duterte's presidency, before courts determined insufficient evidence against her.
Duterte: Filing a case is a right
Paolo Duterte rejected De Lima's criticism Saturday, October 24, arguing that seeking legal redress is not an attack on press freedom.
"Filing a case through the legal process is not an attack on press freedom, but a right available to every citizen," Duterte said in a Cebuano social media post.
Duterte acknowledged the importance of press freedom to democracy but said journalists also have a responsibility to ensure their reports have sufficient basis.
"Reporting an allegation and proving that it is true are two different things," he said. He added that allegations should be addressed through evidence and due process.
Duterte then turned personal in his response, bringing up past allegations against De Lima involving the New Bilibid Prison and saying an accused person has the right to defend himself.
He ended his post with a swipe at De Lima, telling her to stay in Congress, "just keep acting cute there" and "keep smiling for now."

articles.title: ‘You need persistence’: the Norfolk couple who took on environmental regulators three times – and won
articles.summary:
Tim and Geli Harris have spent more than a decade fighting to protect Catfield Fen, a rare wetland in the Norfolk Broads

Polluters and regulators who fail to stop pollution must quake in…

blocks.text: Polluters and regulators who fail to stop pollution must quake in their boots when they receive a letter from the lawyers for Tim and Geli Harris. The couple, who farm 460 acres in the Norfolk Broads, have now scored a hat-trick of landmark legal victories to save an internationally important wetland after they won again in the high court this month.

Lady Justice Lieven found that Natural England failed in its statutory duty to protect Catfield Fen from pollution after nitrates and phosphates washed from arable fields into one of the finest examples of calcareous fen in western Europe, home to 2,500 species including rarities such as the fen orchid, crested buckler fern, breeding bittern and swallowtail butterflies.

In a scathing assessment of Natural England’s inaction since the Harrises first reported the pollution to it in 2021, the judge said the cause of the pollution was “the most basic level of common sense” and required action by the government’s conservation watchdog.

The Harrises have spent 15 years and £1.5m of their own money taking action to hold to account government agencies for failing to protect the fen, which is part of a special area of conservation (SAC), an internationally important wetland protected by law. The marshes lie within the Broads national park.

“This is bigger than a little ditch in Norfolk,” says Tim. He fears that “regulatory inertia” is preventing pollution from being halted on waterways across the country. “Inertia is prevalent throughout all the regulatory bodies. It’s a landmark judgment because it says they can’t just do nothing.”

blocks.caption: Catfield Fen is an internationally important and tremendously diverse wetland.   Photograph: Ali Smith/The Guardian

blocks.text: The couple are big fans of Dirty Business, the recent Channel 4 dramatisation of a maths professor and a retired detective’s battle against sewage pollution, the water companies and the Environment Agency.

“It’s just like that film when you go to a meeting,” Tim says. “The language is from [George Orwell’s] 1984. What we call the light side doesn’t have the money. The dark side does. That’s where the money is. Of course it is.”
“They are slippery snakes,” Geli adds.

Tim held senior roles in the shipping industry, collecting “the wages of sin”, before turning to environmental campaigning in retirement. “She’s the greenie,” he says of Geli, who grew up near the forests around Heidelberg, Germany, and has always loved the natural world.

They bought their farm, which came with a large chunk of Catfield Fen, in 1994, wanting to live closer to nature. They turned their arable fields into pasture to prevent soils and pollution from washing into the fen, and continue to tend English white park cattle, sheep and rare-breed Eriskay ponies.

“It is beautiful,” Geli says of the fen, which requires a careful rotational cut to preserve its rare plants, invertebrates and birdlife. “It’s a little bit of wildness. It’s mysterious. There are places here where we’ve never been – they are pure nature.”
Tim says: “It’s taken 1,000 years to create this and people could destroy it very quickly.” Geli adds: “If you water your plants with the wrong water, they die quite quickly.”

blocks.caption: The Harrises have spent 15 years and £1.5m of their own money holding agencies to account for failing to protect the fen. Photograph: Ali Smith/The Guardian

blocks.text: The Harrises take conservation advice from the experts at Natural England. “We get on well with Natural England, apart from suing them,” Tim says. “They all came to tea and we talked about everything but the thing [the legal case]. It was a very British occasion. They have some very good people. The trouble is too many no longer have fire in their bellies. They are apparatchiks. We respect them but we wish they had more ‘go’.”
Natural England said it accepted the court’s verdict that it had not done enough to protect Catfield Fen but it would not comment on ongoing legal proceedings.

In 2016, the couple won a public inquiry that demonstrated that too much groundwater was being taken from the valley by water companies and local farmers, causing Catfield Fen to dry out. They won a second battle in 2022, forcing the Environment Agency to limit the abstraction of water close to other nature-rich sites on the Norfolk Broads.

Their principles have cost them local friendships. They say National Farmers’ Union reps rejected their application for membership of the local branch, saying half their members would resign, with farmers upset at restrictions on their abstraction of water to boost lucrative crops such as potatoes. “We’re farmers, we’re not anti-farmer,” Tim says.
after newsletter promotion

Since their 2022 legal victory, the Harrises have noticed an improvement in the water levels and biodiversity of Catfield Fen’s dykes. Geli says: “We are a Noah’s ark until things get better and nature can spread outwards from here again.”

blocks.caption: The couple are campaigning to limit water abstraction in the area. Photograph: Si Barber/The Guardian

blocks.text: The fen and its wildlife may be in a better condition under their stewardship, but they are not confident that nature is winning. “The evidence this summer was that the insect numbers are going south, according to the experts who survey here,” Tim says. “We are not complacent; we are very worried.”

The judge is to make further rulings on what Natural England must do to stop the pollution of Catfield Fen. For the Harrises, the answer is simple: arable farmers must be paid to put in buffer strips of grassland between their ploughed fields and the ditches leading to the Broads to reduce the nitrate-filled soils washing from arable fields into the fen.

blocks.caption: The couple are considering another legal challenge. Photograph: Si Barber/The Guardian

blocks.text: More widely, Tim argues that regulatory bodies must simply put their resources into monitoring and compliance. He fears most breaches of environmental rules go unnoticed because of a lack of both.

The Harrises say they do not want to spend their time campaigning. “I don’t want any of this, believe me,” Tim says, gesturing at the box files that take up two walls of shelving. “I’m 79. I want to read books.”

He believes the Broads Authority, the government agency responsible for the national park, should be leading the fight against pollution. Nevertheless, they are considering another legal challenge to stop the Broads from being polluted.

Their stewardship of Catfield Fen will continue after they go. Their daughter will take on the farm, and she is a lawyer by training. So is their granddaughter. “The agencies are not getting rid of the Harrises when we die,” Tim laughs.
Do they hope their example can inspire others to believe they can act to protect nature and clean water? “You need enormous persistence,” Tim says.
“You need passion,” Geli adds. “Evil can happen when people do nothing.”

articles.title: Why sports insider Brian Windhorst’s career begins and ends with writing
articles.summary: ‘No one story is worth damaging a relationship that maybe involves 5, 10, 15 years of building,’ says American sports media personality Brian Windhorst, who visited Manila for the NBA on Disney+’s…

image.caption: Why sports insider Brian Windhorst’s career begins and ends with writing

blocks.text: Brian Windhorst has broken some of the biggest sports stories from the least glamorous places imaginable.
Long before he became a renowned NBA insider and a household name among basketball fans globally, he learned that the news doesn’t wait for a convenient time or location.

Over his 20-year career, Windhorst has taken urgent, league-shifting phone calls in chaotic airport terminals, public bathrooms, and cramped stadium broom closets. He even reported a massive NBA development from a hospital room while waiting for his wife, Maureen Ellen Fulton, to undergo a scheduled cesarean section.
“It wasn’t going to be for an hour, so… you’re just killing time,” Windhorst shared to Rappler during a recent Manila visit.
But somehow, that round-the-clock hustle is what a kid from Akron, Ohio wanted — Windhorst decided early on that a conventional life wasn’t going to cut it.
Today, his globe-trotting career is defined by television appearances, the flash of cameras, and millions of social media followers.
Yet, Windhorst insists that all of it — the television sets, the viral moments, and the multi-million-dollar sports spectacles — isn’t exactly complete without the quiet, grinding work of a writer.

To him, sports journalism operates exactly like a ride at Disneyland: before visitors can climb aboard an attraction, there must be a movie. Before the movie, a character; and before that character ever comes to life, someone has to sit down at a keyboard.
“The character doesn’t exist without the writer,” Windhorst said as The Hoop Collective visited the Philippines to launch NBA on Disney+’s 2026-2027 season.
“It all comes from writing,” he said. “Everything that we do comes from writing. You can never stop writing. I will never stop writing, ever.”
Growing up near Cleveland, Windhorst’s future was once mapped out on an ordinary Saturday with a strict $10 budget.

As a high schooler looking to escape his parents’ conventional nine-to-five routine, he would stretch that budget to cover bus fare, a movie ticket, and his favorite, now-discontinued Taco Bell item: the Chilito. He was just a local kid who wanted to get out, see the world, and chase something grander.
“I wanted to be, at some level, extraordinary,” he said.
Basketball offered him that exact path. While studying journalism at Kent State University, Windhorst fell in love with the specific rhythm of the NBA.
The league’s 82-game regular season offered a perfect balance, providing frequent competition alongside unique opportunities to travel.
But he’ll always remember covering high school basketball in Ohio, where he watched a 14-year-old LeBron James play his first high school game.
Windhorst remembers a tall, lanky teenager with big feet who was still growing into his body. What stood out immediately was how smoothly James moved.
“There’s a lot of tall, you know, teenagers — he was barely a teenager — are awkward,” Windhorst said.. “You know, they don’t move that well when they’re growing so tall. He moved so smooth.”

James scored 15 points that night. Afterward, his coach told Windhorst that James was the best player he had ever coached — a sweeping assessment that the young reporter struggled to believe at the time.
James, of course, became one of basketball’s greatest icons, and Windhorst’s coverage of him became a defining pillar of his own career.
Windhorst readily acknowledges that he would not have reached the same professional heights without James. But the experience also taught him to look beyond the box score.

In 2003, Windhorst began covering the Cleveland Cavaliers for the Akron Beacon Journal. He moved to The Plain Dealer in 2008 before joining ESPN in 2010, bringing behind-the-scenes developments to a national audience.
The relentless nature of his national role affected everyone around him, creating a landscape where work never truly stops.
Windhorst recalls a time when Philadelphia 76ers coach Nick Nurse had to abandon a long-awaited round of golf midway through the course just to take an urgent call from James’ agent.
“Sometimes that’s the nature of this job,” Windhorst noted. “It’s a job that doesn’t have nine-to-five hours.”
Yet, despite the intense pressure to break news first, he insists that speed must never compromise accuracy.
“Being wrong once is way worse than being right a hundred times in a row,” he said.
One of Windhorst’s biggest career scoops arrived when Kyrie Irving suddenly demanded a trade away from the Cleveland Cavaliers in 2017.

The news blindsided the basketball world, but as Windhorst points out, trade reporting rarely begins when a deal is officially announced. It begins months in advance by tracking minor shifts in behavior and recognizing when a situation no longer looks the way it did before.
“The real value for me is: can you say what a team is going to do before they do it, or what they might do?”

Sometimes, that deep reporting translates into unforgettable television. During an episode of ESPN’s First Take, Windhorst delivered a brilliant, dramatic analysis of the Utah Jazz’s future, using precise hand gestures to stress his prediction.

He was 98% sure of an impending trade but couldn’t legally report it as confirmed yet, so he teased it cryptically. Within two hours, his prediction came true, and his dramatic delivery instantly became a viral internet meme.
The sudden internet fame caught him off guard.

“It sort of scares you about social media, in all honesty,” he admitted, noting that the viral moment didn’t replace the actual journalistic grinding required to get the information in the first place.

Another important thing in Windhorst’s line of work is trust. Maintaining deep league relationships means showing up to empty arenas, attending grueling training camps, and remaining present during ugly losing stretches.
As he values trust, he would even prefer to miss a major breaking scoop entirely rather than burn a bridge for a fleeting headline.
“No one story is worth damaging a relationship that maybe involves 5, 10, 15 years of building,” Windhorst said.
“Time. Nobody ever wants to talk about time because they want stuff right away.”
Windhorst deeply admires fellow ESPN journalist Michael Wilbon for the decades of respect he has earned from players, coaches, and owners alike by simply being fair to people.
For Windhorst, that kind of legacy is the goal because the game itself is secondary to the people playing it.
“Ultimately, the game is throwing a ball through a ring,” he said. “That’s all it is. It’s a child’s game. The player’s job is to provide the spectacle. My job is to tell the story.”
And for him, that work will always begin with writing. – Rappler.com
Jade Tan is a Rappler intern studying AB Journalism at University of Santo Tomas, Manila.

articles.title: Opposition deepfake video of Spanish PM’s wife sparks outrage before election
articles.summary:
Video shows AI likenesses of people linked to Pedro Sánchez’s Socialist party appearing to admit to wrongdoing

A political ad from Spain’s main opposition party that used a deepfake video of…

blocks.text: A political ad from Spain’s main opposition party that used a deepfake video of the prime minister’s wife has sparked outrage and set off a wider debate on AI, as the deeply polarised country gears up for general elections next month.

Launched this week across the social media channels of the conservative People’s party (PP), the video used artificial intelligence to manipulate the likenesses of various people linked to Pedro Sánchez’s Socialist party and appeared to show them admitting to acts such as soliciting prostitutes and taking kickbacks.

An AI-generated version of Sánchez’s wife, Begoña Gómez, for example, speaks about receiving a university post thanks to her husband’s job, while a deepfake of the former Socialist president José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero speaks about hiding jewellery in a safe. Both lines are nods to ongoing investigations in which Gómez and Zapatero have denied any wrongdoing.

blocks.caption: A still from the People’s party AI-generated video featuring a deepfake of Begoña Gomez. Computer-generated: @ppopular/X

blocks.text: The Socialist party was swift to respond to the video, which by Friday had racked up nearly 2m views. “It’s telling people a colossal lie, and for a party to do it on its official accounts seems intolerable to me,” Óscar López, Spain’s digital transformation minister, told the broadcaster TVE on Friday.

While the video noted at the bottom – in tiny, nearly transparent font – that it had been created with AI, López pointed to the wider risk. “It’s very easy for anyone who isn’t used to AI to confuse that video with reality,” he said. “And call me crazy, but that seems extremely serious to me.”

On Friday, one of those whose likeness was used in the video filed a legal challenge against the PP, calling on the party to immediately take down the campaign advert. In a court complaint, Leire Díez, a former Socialist party member, reportedly accused the PP of defamation and digital identity theft, after the video used her likeness to hint at accusations that she worked to undermine judicial and law enforcement in order to help the Socialists.

A majority of the nine legal experts consulted by the newspaper El País concurred that what the PP had done was not illegal, given that the video was labelled as AI-generated and that the overall tone was one of political satire. “Given the context, everyone knows those people didn’t say those things,” Íñigo Navarro, a former dean of the faculty of law at Madrid’s Comillas Pontifical University, told the paper.

But the legality of the video was just one aspect, said Juan Antonio Lascuraín, a professor of criminal law at the Autonomous University of Madrid. “It’s quite another matter to ask whether it’s appropriate, exemplary or ethically and politically correct.”
Many sought to contextualise the videos within the wider effort – under way by officials across much of the world – to crack down on the impact of disinformation.

“It’s truly regrettable that the official account of a party that claims to want to govern and revitalise democracy is using AI-generated deepfakes in its campaign,” said José Javier Olivas, an associate professor who researches populism, conspiracy theories and AI biases at Spain’s National University for Distance Education.

He pointed to the wider backdrop of the election campaign, in which both mainstream parties have sought to rally voters by stoking emotions and attacking the morality of their rivals, but he said the video was a “red line” in terms of how campaigns normally unfolded.
after newsletter promotion
“You’re using the images of other people, putting words in their mouths that they’re not saying, [and] this qualifies for disinformation,” he said.

The use of AI to generate or enhance political ads has also become a talking point in the US ahead of next month’s midterm elections. A recent report by a research group based at Wesleyan University in Connecticut identified more than 200 such ads, the vast majority of them tied to the Republicans.

“AI is making its way into the 2026 midterms in a big way this year,” said Erika Franklin Fowler, a co-director of the Wesleyan Media Project. “For comparison, we identified less than $50,000 in spending on AI-generated ads in the 2024 cycle. Much of the AI use is not disclosed through any type of disclaimer.”

In Spain, the PP has brushed off criticism. “If there had been malicious intent to make people believe that the characters who appear there are real, then we’d have a problem,” Borja Sémper, of the party, told reporters. “But everyone can see that this is a way of using digital tools to highlight the hypocrisy in which the Socialist party operates.”
Most polls suggest the PP will win the 29 November general election but will need to rely on the support of the far-right Vox party to form a government.

articles.title: LTFRB warns taxi drivers vs overcharging, snubbing passengers amid Undas exodus
articles.summary: As the public began traveling to their hometowns for Undas, the Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board warned taxi drivers of penalties for overcharging fares, snubbing, and…

blocks.text: Published October 24, 2026 2:37pm

As the public began traveling to their hometowns for Undas, the Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board (LTFRB) warned taxi drivers of penalties for overcharging fares, snubbing, and disrespecting passengers during the All Saints’ Day break.

In a press release on Saturday, LTFRB Acting Chairman Atty. Greg Pua Jr. warned that violations of the agency’s rules and regulations could lead to the suspension or cancellation of a Certificate of Public Convenience, among other penalties.

“We expect more passengers going to bus terminals and other major transportation hubs starting next week. This early, we are giving a fair warning to all taxi operators to behave and stick to the rules and regulations of the authority to operate issued to them,” Pua said.
The Parañaque Integrated Terminal Exchange (PITX) previously stated that it is expecting around 1.9 million passengers for this year’s exodus for All Saints' Day.
Meanwhile, up to 2 million passengers are expected at seaports, according to the Philippine Coast Guard.
The LTFRB added that it similarly expects an influx of passengers at major bus terminals in Quezon City, Manila, Pasay City, Caloocan City, and Muntinlupa.
The agency stated that it will actively monitor complaints on social media platforms and conduct surprise inspections using mystery riders.

“The LTFRB is in full force when it comes to monitoring. This should serve as a strong message to both operators and drivers that we are watching you, and that you know what would happen if we catch you,” Pua said.
Pua advised passengers to report any incidents of abuse to LTFRB Hotline 1342 or through the agency’s official social media accounts. —Lyjah Tiffany Bonzo/KG, GMA News

blocks.text: What you need to know

items: Hundreds of thousands of people are expected to take to France's streets to protest over the rising cost of living, declining social services and inequality
Authorities are looking to prevent a repeat of the violence that took place at similar protests a week ago with heightened security and bans
President Emmanuel Macron has called a shooting near Paris in which one person died and five were injured 'a racist terrorist attack'
Protests are also expected in eight Italian cities, including Rome and Milan

blocks.text: Follow below for the latest on the protests and unrest in France and other parts of Europe on Saturday, October 24, 2026:
October 24, 2026
France puts high security in place for fresh protests

French authorities say they will be deploying some 70,000 police on Saturday amid renewed protests as they look to prevent a repeat of the violence that marred mass nationwide demonstrations over social inequality a week ago.
Announcing the deployment, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez warned at a news conference in Paris that calls for violence and looting were circulating on social media.

Several restrictions on protests have been imposed across the country, including bans on a union-led march on one route in the capital, Paris, that organizers say they will disregard, citing safety concerns about a proposed alternative.
Leading museums in Paris, including the Louvre, will also remained closed.
The protests come a critical political moment for France, with elections due in six months to elect a successor to President Emmanual Macron.
Polls have shown far-right candidate Marine Le Pen as the frontrunner and indicated that the latest events might have shored up her popularity.
You can read more about the security precautions and background to the protests in France in this article:France to deploy 70,000 police officers ahead of protests

blocks.text: October 24, 2026 | 2:26pm

Veteran journalist Philip Lustre Jr. is escorted by police officers at the Quezon City Police District (QCPD) Kamuning Station 10 in Quezon City to undergo physical and medical examination following his arrest on Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026.
The STAR / Miguel de Guzman
MANILA, Philippines — Police arrested veteran journalist Philip Lustre Jr. while he was attending a media forum in Quezon City on Saturday, October 24, over a cyber libel case filed in Davao City.
Officers from the Quezon City Police District's Station 10 took Lustre into custody, acting on a warrant issued by Davao City Regional Trial Court Branch 10, state-run Radyo Pilipinas reported.
Lustre's lawyer, Dino De Leon, said his client was unaware of the case before the arrest. He added that police had no information on who filed the complaint.
De Leon said Lustre's camp would post P48,000 bail and seek the reopening of the preliminary investigation.
Lustre was brought to the QCPD Kamuning Station 10 for booking and underwent physical and medical examinations.

Lustre is a longtime journalist and critic of the Duterte family. He wrote "Kill, Kill, Kill," a book about former President Rodrigo Duterte's war on drugs. — with reports from The STAR / Miguel de Guzman

articles.title: Blaze engulfs Hitler’s ‘Eagle’s Nest’ mountain retreat in Bavaria
articles.summary:
About 200 firefighters deployed to tackle the blaze at former Nazi retreat in a remote part of southern Germany

German police said Saturday they had detained a suspect after a fire at Adolf…

blocks.text: German police said Saturday they had detained a suspect after a fire at Adolf Hitler’s former mountain retreat, known as the Eagle’s Nest, in the state of Bavaria.
About 200 firefighters were deployed to tackle the blaze at the Nazi dictator’s remote and difficult-to-access Kehlsteinhaus residence, on the peak of Obersalzberg in southern Germany.
Firefighters saw flames rising high into the air as they approached the scene, only to find the building “completely ablaze”, police said.
“A suspicious person was taken into temporary custody,” they said in a later statement, adding that nobody was injured in the blaze.
Police spokesperson Lisa Maier said firefighters struggled to tackle the fire due to its location at an altitude of 1,834 metres (6,000 feet).
The building was only accessible with “heavy breathing apparatus”, she said.
Authorities were alerted to the fire on Friday evening, when a smoke detector triggered a fire alarm at about 9.50pm (1950 GMT), police said.
No potential reason for the fire was given, but the German media reported that the investigators suspected it was the result of arson.
As snow fell on the Alpine peak, the Eagle’s Nest was still engulfed in flames in the early hours of Saturday, a weather camera showed.
Officers blocked access to the road leading to the retreat, according to an AFP photographer.
The firefighters found no one inside the building.
Maier said police were still investigating but will hold a news conference later on Saturday.
German tabloid Bild reported that the authorities had arrested a motorcyclist they came across on their way to the scene.

Built between 1937 and 1938, the Eagle’s Nest forms part of the toxic legacy of Hitler’s Third Reich, which was responsible for the deaths of millions of Jews as well as Roma, LGBTQ people and Communists in the Holocaust.
It was designed to serve as a monument to Hitler’s rule, although the dictator rarely visited the complex.
It survived the second world war undamaged, and since 1952 has hosted an exhibition recounting the house’s Nazi history and a restaurant.

articles.title: More than third of post offices in TG Jones stores to shut by early 2027
articles.summary:
Closures within chain formerly under the WH Smith brand raise fears of high streets becoming ‘postal deserts’

Towns and even city centres face being left as “postal deserts” after it emerged…

blocks.text: Towns and even city centres face being left as “postal deserts” after it emerged that more than a third of post offices within the troubled TG Jones chain are closing.

So far this year 36 branches within the high street chain formerly known as WH Smith have closed and a further 34 are set to close by early 2027, according to Post Office records analysed by the Guardian.

TG Jones was bought and renamed by Modella last year. Before the private equity group’s restructure won approval from creditors in July, the chain operated 180 post offices and it had been feared that as many as 60 could be closed under the shake-up.

Up to 150 of the 450 stores acquired by Modella are expected to shut, about 65 of which have already closed and at least another 46 are to cease operating early next year. This total of 110 announced closures include the 70 containing post offices.

The larger-than-expected wave of TG Jones branch closures follows an announcement in the summer that 52 post offices will close within Morrisons Daily convenience stores this year, some of which are close to the TG Jones sites. The move forms part of a wider plan by Morrisons to close 100 loss-making small stores.

The raft of closures means that towns such as Stevenage in Hertfordshire, Bracknell in Berkshire and Orpington in Greater London, and some smaller cities including Hull and York are each losing two post offices in a matter of months. Telford’s last one is due to close in January.

The majority of these lost sites replaced former crown post offices, the now almost entirely closed network of more than 100 directly operated large branches, which offered a full suite of services such as identity and passport checks, driving licence and banking operations.

Some regions such as Essex, the West Midlands, Wales, Suffolk and Hertfordshire have been particularly hard hit. Six post offices in TG Jones stores in Essex are going, with Clacton-on-Sea and Brentwood shutting in January after the closure of ones in Basildon, Southend-on-Sea, Harlow and East Ham. Five are closing in the West Midlands and four in Wales.

The Post Office is trying to find new operators in these locations but so far only Stirling has reopened after a TG Jones closure, and a permanent replacement for Ipswich is set to open in November. Temporary branches are to operate after TG Jones closures in Maidenhead and Uxbridge.

Such losses can be devastating to the health of local economies. As the Post Office itself pointed out to a parliamentary inquiry into revitalising high streets, almost a third of small- and medium-sized businesses use their local branch at least once a week and more than half use the network at least once a month. Many small businesses report that losing this access would threaten their viability within months.

After the closure of more than 6,800 bank branches across the UK, the Post Office “plays a critical role in protecting this essential service”, according to thetstate-owned company’s evidence to the inquiry. Post office operators already run 250 banking hubs, which combine services for several banking brands, across the UK.
Mole Meade, a senior member at the CWU, the largest union for postal workers, said the closures would leave some areas as “postal deserts”.

Meade added: “What we are seeing with the TG Jones closures is the continuation of a long-term strategy of cutting costs and chasing profit, with little regard for the communities that depend on post office services.
after newsletter promotion
“The CWU believes the Post Office should be focused on protecting and expanding access to services, not presiding over a continued reduction of the network.”

The Post Office said: “We fully recognise the challenging trading conditions that TG Jones and many other high street retailers are facing at the moment. We proactively sought expressions of interest from our postmasters and partners to take on post offices within TG Jones stores that may close as a result of their restructuring plan or any decisions taken by landlords.

“There is interest in taking on every location where it has been confirmed that a post office within a TG Jones store will close. In some locations there are over 40 applications from our postmasters who recognise the significant footfall operating a post office brings to their store … We’re committed to replacing every branch within a TG Jones store that closes and are working to progress applications as quickly as possible.”
The state-owned Post Office – which is still reeling from the Horizon IT scandal – announced the closure of more than 100 branches in late 2024.
WH Smith travel stores in railway stations, hospitals and airports were not part of the Modella deal and remain owned by its original stock market-listed parent company.
TG Jones was approached for comment.

articles.title: ‘It’s part of our history’: can the menú del día survive Spain’s changing eating habits?
articles.summary:
Established under the Franco dictatorship, the lunchtime ritual is in decline but all is not lost

A little before lunchtime each working day across Spain, evidence of one of the lingering,…

blocks.text: A little before lunchtime each working day across Spain, evidence of one of the lingering, if less notorious, legacies of the Franco dictatorship is carefully traced in chalk, marker pen and printer ink.

Beckoning to hungry workers from blackboards, whiteboards and pieces of paper hastily taped to windows, the competitively priced menú del día, or daily set-price lunch, has been part of everyday Spanish life for more than half a century. But while 4m menús are still served each weekday, Spain is slowly losing its appetite for the familiar ritual.

Back in 2009, the country’s best-known chef, Ferran Adrià, went so far as to pronounce it dead – a victim of changing eating habits, economic downturns and bistro-style restaurants trying to charge €20-€30 (£17-£25) for what should be a simple starter, a hearty main and a choice of pudding or coffee … with bread and a drink thrown in.

Seventeen years later, however, the diagnosis seem a little premature. A new book by the Spanish food journalist Lakshmi Aguirre charts the history and evolution of the menú and argues that while the tradition is indeed in hot water, it hasn’t quite had its chips.

Her book – Menú del Día: Everyday Scenes of a First Course, a Second Course and Pudding – begins with the unpalatable fact that it all began with a tourist menu dreamed up in the mid-1960s up by the Spanish dictator Francisco Franco’s information and tourism minister, Manuel Fraga.

The regime was keen in the aftermath of the “years of hunger” that followed the Spanish civil war to show foreign visitors that food was plentiful, good and affordable. So it was that establishments serving food should offer “a starter of soup, a main course chosen from at least three options and based on egg, fish or meat and accompanied by a side dish, and a pudding based on fruit, something sweet, or cheese”.

blocks.caption: A selection of daily menus on chalkboards in Madrid. They typically consist of a simple starter, a hearty main and a choice of pudding or coffee with bread and a drink thrown in.

blocks.text: The price was set at between 50 and 250 pesetas and, to stop unscrupulous restaurant owners watering down the drinks, the law stipulated that the accompanying quarter-litre of vino had to be “reds and whites from Spain that are pure, clean, pleasant on the palate and with an alcohol content of not less than 12%”.

In the early 1970s, the menú del día was rebaptised to make it look less like an attempt to woo – and sometimes gouge – tourists, but also to give ordinary Spaniards the idea that they, too, could indulge.

It is now so ubiquitous that many in Spain have no idea of its genesis. “When I was working on the book and people asked me about the menú del día, I’d mention Manuel Fraga and lots of them would throw their hands up in shock,” Aguirre said. “Some people know, but the vast majority don’t. It says a lot about us Spaniards; we forget very quickly.”
Researching the book, which includes personal reminiscences and a hefty selection of recipes, led Aguirre to consider the place of the menú in the popular consciousness.

“It’s part of our history, yet it’s changed over the years, reflecting the evolution of Spanish society,” she said. “It originated from something as terrible as a dictatorship, and today it has become a deeply ingrained custom. We feel a sense of nostalgia as we realise it’s fading away.”

blocks.caption: Aguirre says restaurants serving a menú del día should be a centre of community gravity ‘where families with limited financial means can afford to eat out’. Photograph: Jeffrey Isaac Greenberg/Alamy

blocks.text: The threats to the set lunch, whose average price today is €14.70, are many. Increasingly time-poor, many Spaniards now opt for a quick lunch, eating food from home at work or popping to a supermarket for a ready meal to microwave in a soulless canteen. Rising energy and food prices are making it harder for small, family-run restaurants to offer a rotating daily selection of starters and mains.

All of which explains the rise of the “dish of the day”, which offers restaurants a cheaper alternative to the traditional choice of three or four mains, and the increasing diversity of some menús, which now feature Latin American staples as a reflection of Spain’s changing demographics.

“The menú del día purists reject such options, but it has always been a reflection of the society that consumes it – and that’s exactly how it should be,” Aguirre said. “Spain today isn’t the same as it was in the 1980s, it is far more diverse and pluralistic, and as a result diners have changed as well. The menú del día exists for those who need it, for people who may come from many different backgrounds.”
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: A daily menu at a restaurant in Palma, Mallorca. The food writer Lakshmi Aguirre says chalkboards should ideally be written by ‘someone who’s never heard of lettering’. Photograph: Ian Shaw/Alamy

blocks.text: Aguirre’s menú of choice would be a simple but well-cooked vegetable stew followed by hake in green sauce or baby squid in ink, and then leche frita (fried custard) or rice pudding.

But, as she points out in her book, the surroundings are almost as important as the cooking. Her benchmarks for a good menú del día spot include simple dishes, a regularly changing menu, chips that aren’t frozen, a chorus of regulars and “a chalkboard free of any trace of words such as avocado, burrata, tartare, truffle or sourdough bread”.
That chalkboard should, by preference, be written “by someone who’s never heard of lettering”, and bonus points are awarded if the child of the owners is doing their homework on a table down the end.
As it hobbles slowly towards what may be its demise, the menú del día has become something that transcends a filling and reasonably priced midday meal.

“What’s being lost is a meeting point,” Aguirre said. “A centre of community gravity where families with limited financial means can afford to eat out, and where those who live alone can find some company during a meal, which remains a deeply social activity.

“It’s a place where joys, sorrows and problems can be shared, or where you can simply enjoy a bit of breathing space, as well as a place for those who live far away or who don’t have the time to go home for lunch.”
The true privilege of the menú, she added, lay “not just in being able to pay for a meal, but also in having the time to enjoy it”.

articles.title: FBI, Philippine authorities probe Meghan Markle's dad over alleged abuse images
articles.summary: A Philippine task force in Cebu is investigating allegations against Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex.

blocks.text: October 24, 2026 | 1:57pm

LONDON, United Kingdom — Prince Harry's wife Meghan said Friday, October 23 she was "deeply distressed" by accusations her father had possessed images of child abuse allegedly found among his belongings at his former home in the Philippines.
The Sun and Daily Mail newspapers reported the allegations against her estranged father Thomas Markle. He denies all the claims.
A spokesperson for the FBI said it was "aware of the allegations and will provide support, as appropriate, to the Philippine authorities".
"We will also investigate any related allegations of federal violations of US law," its statement added.

Agence France Presse has reached out to the police in the Philippines for a comment, as the Daily Mail said it was Thomas Markle's son, Meghan's half-brother Thomas Markle Jr, who had discovered the images and reported them to local police.
Thomas Markle, who now reportedly lives in a rehab center in Florida, told the Daily Mail the allegations against him were "sick lies".
After the reports, Meghan revealed that in 2018 she had seen a letter sent to London's Metropolitan Police and Royalty and Specialist Protection making similar accusations.
"It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated," she said in a statement.
However, a source close to the matter said the Met Police had not and was not investigating the matter.
A Met Police statement said it was "undertaking enquiries internally in an effort to confirm" what the duchess said about the letter.
Thomas Markle moved from Mexico to Cebu in 2025, settling there with his son Thomas Markle Jr., according to media reports at the time.
Markle reportedly returned to the United States in May 2026 for further medical care and a prosthetic limb.
'Protect'
"I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed," Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, said in the statement.
Meghan and Harry have two children, Archie, seven, and Lilibet, five.

The duchess said she hoped it could "now be understood that, despite certain media publications' distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them".

"Although the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine, my sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children," Meghan added.
Estranged
Harry, the second son of King Charles III and estranged brother of heir to the throne Prince William, married the former American actress at Windsor Castle in May 2018.
Thomas Markle did not attend. The PA news agency reported the letter was seen by his daughter in mid-2018, after the wedding.
He pulled out of Harry and Meghan's wedding due to heart surgery amid a furore after he was found to have received payment for staged paparazzi photographs.
It later emerged that father and daughter remained estranged and that Markle had never met his grandchildren.
In December, however, a spokesperson for Meghan said she had been in touch with her father who was in a Philippines hospital after having a leg amputated.

In 2021, Meghan won a UK High Court privacy and copyright claim against Daily Mail publisher Associated Newspapers over articles that reproduced parts of a "private" letter she wrote to him, asking him to stop talking to the press.
The couple left Britain and quit royal duties in 2020 amid a royal family feud.
They made an unexpected return with their children to live in the United Kingdom in August. — Based on reports from Agence France Presse

articles.title: Lacson says TESDA offered him P5-M 'allocation fund,' but agency denies claim
articles.summary: Senator Panfilo "Ping" Lacson on Saturday said the Technical Education and Skills Development Authority (TESDA) offered him a P5-million "allocation fund," but the agency rejected the claim.

blocks.text: Published October 24, 2026 1:56pm
Senator Panfilo "Ping" Lacson on Saturday said the Technical Education and Skills Development Authority (TESDA) offered him a P5-million "allocation fund," but the agency rejected the claim.
In a statement, Lacson said the proposal was made through his Senate staff earlier this week, but he refused it.
The senator said he would clarify the issue when TESDA's proposed 2027 budget is tackled in the Senate plenary next month.

"When TESDA's proposed 2027 budget comes up for plenary debate, I will seek clarification on the P5-million fund offer made to me through my Senate staff early this week. I declined unequivocally," Lacson said.

Lacson posted on his X account the screenshot of the alleged allocation fund offer from TESDA Secretary and Director General Jose Francisco Benitez, which was supposedly channeled through an individual named "Stephanie."
Lacson said he initially considered an entrapment or sting operation against those involved in the transaction, but took pity on "Stephanie."

"Maybe they thought I'm 'standard practice.' They didn't know me. Now they do. Initially, I considered entrapment, but I took pity on Stephanie who apparently was only following instructions," Lacson said.
Lacson earlier said the Senate would examine the House-approved version of the 2027 budget bill, and address the red flags there, including those related to Foreign-Assisted Projects (FAPs).

When TESDA's proposed 2027 budget comes up for plenary debate, I will seek clarification on the P5-million fund offer made to me through my Senate staff early this week. I declined unequivocally. https://t.co/J1WcjC97RG— PING LACSON (@iampinglacson) October 23, 2026
In a statement, however, the TESDA chief denied giving the go-ahead for such an offer.
"As TESDA Secretary, I did not authorize anyone to offer any allocation or one amounting to P5 million to Senator Ping Lacson," Benitez said.

"We thank the Senator for promptly informing us of these misrepresentations. We welcome the opportunity to get to the bottom of this matter and fully support efforts to establish the facts," he added.
Benitez lauded Lacson for the senator's advocacy for good governance, transparency, and accountability, values which he said are also shared by TESDA.

"Given that it's budget season, TESDA routinely reaches out to members of the Senate to inquire if they have concerns with the agency. Any improper offer, allocation, or solicitation in TESDA funds, or any other unauthorized arrangement, involving any legislator is contrary to this Office's directives," he said.

Benitez said the agency had already ordered an immediate internal investigation to identify those responsible for any unauthorized actions or misrepresentations, and enforce appropriate administrative and, if warranted, criminal cases. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Moonshot curbs hacking ability in new Kimi model as fears grow over AI-powered cyberattacks
articles.summary: Moonshot says it removed cyber-related data from the training corpus and reinforcement-learning environments used to develop the model, while retaining general coding skills

blocks.text: MOONSHOT AI. The Moonshot AI logo is seen in this illustration taken September 5, 2026.
Dado Ruvic/Reuters
Moonshot says it removed cyber-related data from the training corpus and reinforcement-learning environments used to develop the model, while retaining general coding skills

items: Moonshot AI has introduced the Kimi K3.1 Pro model with reduced cyber-offensive capabilities by removing cyber-related data from its training, aiming to mitigate hacking risks.
The company plans to publish the model's weights by November 4, allowing developers to run and modify it, while emphasizing that open-weight models can enhance security for organizations.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

Moonshot AI has reduced the cyber-offensive capabilities of its newest model, the Chinese startup said on Saturday, October 24, as fears grow that increasingly autonomous AI could turbocharge hacking.

Beijing-based Moonshot announced the curbs while introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro, which it describes as its most capable 3-trillion-parameter-class open-weight model. The company plans to publish the model’s weights — files allowing outside developers to run and modify it on their own systems — by November 4.
Moonshot said it removed cyber-related data from the training corpus and reinforcement-learning environments used to develop the model, while retaining general coding skills.
“We aim not to release open weights that would extend the absolute frontier of cyber capability,” the company said.

Governments, technology companies and security researchers are growing increasingly concerned that AI could make sophisticated hacking easier and cheaper. Models that can write code, operate software tools and complete long, multi-step tasks may help users identify weaknesses in programs and automate parts of cyberattacks.

blocks.caption: Millions of hacking attempts as companies, governments rush to patch PHP flaws

blocks.text: China proposed export controls last week that would ban exports of AI-driven malware-generation and mutation technology and restrict AI-assisted vulnerability-discovery tools. The draft measures, which remain open for public comment, cite the risk that such capabilities could be used against critical infrastructure, defence-industrial and core government systems, or to bypass security protections.
Moonshot said open-weight models can improve security by helping more organisations inspect and secure their own software, including older systems that receive little attention.

Unlike proprietary, closed-weight AI systems, however, open-weight releases make central oversight more difficult. Once the files are widely distributed, the original developer has less ability to restrict access, monitor use or update safeguards than with a hosted service.

K3.1 Pro scored 81.0% on its internal cyber benchmark, compared with 90.5% for a similar version without the risk-reduction measures, the company said. The test involved finding and exploiting software vulnerabilities in a controlled environment. Moonshot said the comparison showed that filtering cyber-related data reduced the model’s offensive cyber performance, although it still outperformed its predecessor. The results have not been independently verified.

K3.1 Pro has a 1-million-token context window, allowing it to process very large amounts of text at once. Moonshot also released a faster version, K3.1 Pro Highspeed, which it said runs at two to three times the speed of the standard model. – Rappler.com
