articles.title: Sherwin: Recall of House budget bill unnecessary
articles.summary: Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian yesterday rejected calls from the Makabayan bloc in the House of Representatives to recall the chamber’s budget bill for 2027, saying that the Senate would…

blocks.text: October 24, 2026 | 12:00am
Senator Sherwin Gatchalian..
STAR / Ryan Baldemor

MANILA, Philippines — Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian yesterday rejected calls from the Makabayan bloc in the House of Representatives to recall the chamber’s budget bill for 2027, saying that the Senate would make the necessary corrections to ensure constitutional compliance without risking a reenacted budget.

House Deputy Minority Leader Antonio Tinio and his Makabayan colleagues recently urged Congress to pull the House-approved version of the 2027 budget from the Senate, arguing that it contains provisions that mirror elements struck down by the Supreme Court, including questionable triggers for unprogrammed appropriations and prohibited lump-sum allocations.

“I think it’s important and necessary so that the House can clean up its own mess, because if you look at the budget passed by the House, there are significant parts that could be declared unconstitutional as well,” Tinio explained. “We don’t want yet another budget that will be declared unconstitutional.”
However, Gatchalian dismissed the necessity of recall, explaining that the Senate is already positioned to correct these flaws during its consolidation and committee report process.
“Not necessary because we are entering the consolidation of the budget here so we can do the correction ourselves,” Gatchalian told reporters.

“Rest assured, the 2027 budget will be compliant with [the] Constitution,” Gatchalian said, adding that the 2027 budget would not mirror the unconstitutional provisions flagged by the high court in the 2024 and 2025 budgets.

Meanwhile, Sen. Panfilo Lacson warned that returning the budget bill to the House would likely result in a reenacted budget – a scenario that he described as “worse” because it operates on lump sums without itemized provisions.
“That is not the solution. The solution is for the Senate to really scrutinize and cut all the fat sent in the GAB [General Appropriations Bill] of the House. That is the solution,” Lacson said.
He suggested Makabayan bloc lawmakers should instead raise their concerns with their House colleagues who would eventually sit in the bicameral conference committee.
Senate budget
In a bid to set an example for fiscal discipline, Lacson revealed that the Senate plans to slash its own proposed budget by P2 billion.

“In fact, we agreed with the Senate President the other day, me being the chairman of the committee on accounts, we will reduce our budget, the Senate budget, by about P2 billion from the NEP [National Expenditure Program],” Lacson disclosed.
He pointed out the contrast between the two chambers, noting that while the House added P5 billion to its own allocation, the Senate is taking the opposite route.

Lacson gave assurance that the P2-billion cut – which will bring the Senate’s budget down to P5 billion from the proposed P7 billion – will not disrupt the chamber’s operations, as there are still unused funds available.

Gatchalian said the Senate is also addressing red flags in the House version, particularly concerning infrastructure insertions, with some farm-to-market road projects proposed by the House having been plotted in the middle of the ocean.
“There are coordinates there that is in the Benham Rise or in the Middle East. So we have to check. I’m sure it’s a typo,” Gatchalian said.
The Senate President added they have already flagged the Department of Agriculture regarding these errors and duplicate project entries.
Lacson noted that the Senate’s decision to invite civil society organizations as resource persons during the budget hearings has been instrumental in exposing these anomalies. – Delon Porcalla

articles.title: Diesel price hike looms; rollback for gasoline
articles.summary: Motorists should brace for another increase in diesel prices next week as escalating hostilities in the Middle East threaten to further disrupt global oil supplies.

blocks.text: October 24, 2026 | 12:00am
MANILA, Philippines — Motorists should brace for another increase in diesel prices next week as escalating hostilities in the Middle East threaten to further disrupt global oil supplies.

Based on the first four days of trading in the Mean of Platts Singapore, the regional benchmark for refined petroleum products in the Asia-Pacific, diesel prices are projected to rise by P2 to P2.50 per liter.
Gasoline prices, meanwhile, could drop by P1 to P1.50 per liter.
The projected adjustments remain preliminary as they do not yet account for week-on-week changes in freight costs.
Jetti Petroleum president Leo Bellas said oil prices rallied amid mounting supply concerns following intensified Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure and vessels.
“Loadings outside of the Arab Gulf are now threatened as well, jeopardizing Gulf crude loadings and ship-to-ship transfers that helped support regional loadings,” Bellas said.
Market anxiety has also been fueled by fears of further escalation in geopolitical tensions following the US midterm elections.
For refined petroleum products, diesel prices have come under additional upward pressure from declining oil flows and intensified Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries.
“Meanwhile, rising gasoline inventories in Singapore pointed to an improving product availability in Asia,” Bellas said.
He added that persistent tightness in diesel supplies has encouraged refiners to maintain crude processing rates, potentially helping sustain gasoline supply even as demand weakens.
The Department of Energy is expected to announce the prescribed pump price adjustments on Monday.
Strategic oil reserves

Amid continuing oil price volatility, lawmakers are pushing for the creation of a Philippine Strategic Petroleum Reserve System to help shield consumers and businesses from supply disruptions and sharp price increases.
Camarines Sur Reps. Migz Villafuerte and Luigi Villafuerte urged yesterday their colleagues in the House of Representatives to support House Bill 9367, which seeks to establish the reserve system.
The measure was also authored by Rep. Tsuyoshi Anthony Horibata and Bicol Saro party-list Rep. Terry Ridon.
The lawmakers explained that the country’s dependence on imported petroleum products leaves it vulnerable to global market fluctuations, underscoring the need for government-controlled fuel reserves.

“Despite its heavy reliance on imported petroleum products, our country lacks a comprehensive legal framework establishing a government-controlled strategic petroleum reserve that will protect Filipinos and businesses from wild swings in the prices of diesel, gasoline and other petroleum products,” Luigi said.
Migz, meanwhile, noted that countries with established strategic petroleum reserves could draw on their stocks during supply disruptions and periods of severe price volatility.

“The Philippines has no comparable government-controlled strategic petroleum reserve to draw from during a major supply disruption and thus remains largely exposed to market volatility, relying instead on commercial inventories and external supply conditions,” he said.

The proposed framework would cover the acquisition, storage, maintenance, rotation and emergency release of petroleum reserves. It would also allow the Department of Energy to work with private entities through public-private partnerships to develop and operate reserve facilities.

The push for legislation comes as Maharlika Investment Corp. and the Philippine National Oil Co. have signed a memorandum of understanding to evaluate the development, financing and operation of a strategic tank farm in Bataan.
The PNOC is targeting the facility’s operations to begin by 2028, with an initial capacity of one million barrels that could eventually expand to 15 million barrels.
Illegal fuel
Meanwhile, Metro Manila police have intensified operations against illegal fuel trading amid concerns that unscrupulous sellers could exploit supply uncertainties.
Metro Manila police officer-in-charge Brig. Gen. Christopher Abrahano ordered police intelligence units and station commanders to strengthen monitoring and validation of unauthorized fuel trading.
The directive followed the arrest of four individuals by Quezon City police on Tuesday for allegedly selling 172 liters of petroleum products illegally beside a gasoline station in Payatas.

“While the government is working to ensure a sufficient and stable fuel supply for our country, we will not allow illegal traders to take advantage of the situation for their own gain,” Abrahano said. – Delon Porcalla, EJ Macababbad

articles.title: P50 million bounty up for Bato’s capture
articles.summary: Saying the gloves are off, the government has put up a P50-million bounty for any information that will lead to the capture of Sen. Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa, and gave him a week to…

blocks.text: October 24, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — Saying the gloves are off, the government has put up a P50-million bounty for any information that will lead to the capture of Sen. Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa, and gave him a week to surrender. In announcing the reward, Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla said the senator, who is considered “armed and dangerous,” has been given all the courtesy to voluntarily surrender following an International Criminal Court (ICC) warrant of arrest issued in November 2025.
Dela Rosa, a former Philippine National Police (PNP) chief, has been tagged a co-conspirator of former president Rodrigo Duterte in the crimes against humanity case before the ICC.
Instead of showing up and taking responsibility for his actions, Remulla said Dela Rosa is a coward by remaining in hiding.

“Senator Bato mistook my gesture of negotiation as a sign of weakness. It’s time for the gloves to come off. It’s time to bring justice to his victims,” Remulla told a news briefing at Camp Crame yesterday.
“As of today, Senator Bato will be considered armed and dangerous. We are placing a bounty of P50 million for his capture,” Remulla said.

With the reward, Dela Rosa is now the No. 1 most wanted fugitive in the country, followed by gambling tycoon Charlie “Atong” Ang, who has a P20-million bounty for his arrest in connection with the alleged kidnapping and killing of cockfight enthusiasts or sabungeros.
The bounty for Dela Rosa was sourced from the intelligence funds of the DILG and the PNP, Remulla said.
Remulla has designated PNP deputy chief for administration Lt. Gen. Wilson Lopez as the head of a special task force to arrest Dela Rosa.
PNP chief Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. said Dela Rosa has one week to surrender but maintained law enforcement operations to arrest the senator are ongoing.
Apart from intelligence operatives, Nartatez said they are also utilizing tactical teams and other resources to locate and arrest Dela Rosa.
“With or without ultimatum, with or without reward, the PNP is ready to implement whatever (needs) to be implemented. That is our commitment,” he said.
Dela Rosa is allegedly being protected by a powerful armed group in a secluded area in Mindanao, the reason why Remulla is cautious about launching an operation to arrest the senator by force.
The DILG chief said a bloodbath similar to the siege of Marawi in 2017 could ensue.
For Nartatez, the possibility of casualties is always there but maintained they have contingency measures in place to ensure the lawmaker is caught.
“For example, the coddlers are 10 (people), then we will need a hundred (operatives). It will be a calibrated one,” Nartatez said.

The PNP has searched several areas in Mindanao and Luzon, including Metro Manila, where there have been reported sightings of Dela Rosa but all turned out negative. Nartatez said they could not see a pattern on Dela Rosa’s movements. Nartatez warned Dela Rosa’s coddlers to stop protecting Dela Rosa and hand him over to authorities or face criminal cases.
Dela Rosa’s last public appearance was on May 14, when he was seen exiting the Senate premises alongside Sen. Robinhood Padilla, his colleague in the minority.
Local warrant first
Dela Rosa’s counsel Israelito Torreon rejected the DILG’s bounty for his client, saying a local warrant must first exist.
Torreon’s law firm made a lengthy post on social media yesterday, after the lawyer initially said “no comment” on the matter.
“A reward system built on Philippine warrants cannot be used for a person who has no Philippine warrant,” the law firm of Torreon & Partners posted on Facebook.

“The only document the government has is a warrant from the International Criminal Court. That is a foreign tribunal under a treaty the Philippines withdrew from effective March 17, 2019. No Philippine judge has examined that warrant, adopted it or issued one of his own,” Torreon claimed. – Ghio Ong

articles.title: ICC prosecutor wants more recorded testimonies admitted
articles.summary: The Office of the Prosecutor of the International Criminal Court has requested six more prior recorded testimonies of witnesses to be admitted in the crimes against humanity case against former…

blocks.text: October 24, 2026 | 12:00am
Photos courtesy of the International Criminal Court show former president Rodrigo Duterte during his first in-person appearance before the tribunal since his arrest in March 2025.
Photos / ICC | via Janvic Mateo

MANILA, Philippines — The Office of the Prosecutor of the International Criminal Court (ICC) has requested six more prior recorded testimonies of witnesses to be admitted in the crimes against humanity case against former president Rodrigo Duterte.

Acting prosecutor Mame Mandiaye Niang filed two separate requests seeking the admission of recorded testimonies of witnesses who he said would cover details of Duterte’s drug war, including alleged extrajudicial killings.
This brings the total number of witnesses covered by requests for admission of prior recorded testimonies to 15.
The first of the two new requests, originally filed on Oct. 12, covered witnesses P-0024, P-1357 and P-1359.
Niang said their testimonies primarily relate to the contextual elements of crimes against humanity.
He said their testimonies are suitable for formal submission in written form as they are “cumulative or corroborative nature.”

Based on the filing, P-0024’s written testimony will cover the legal process surrounding the drug war. P-1357 focuses on matters relating to the Davao death squad, while P-1359 discussed the increase in drug-related shooting incidents following Duterte’s election as president.
Meanwhile, the latest set of witnesses were covered in the Oct. 19 filing made public on Oct. 23.
Unlike the previous three, the prosecution still intends to present witnesses P-0008, P-1164 and P- 1303 even if their prior recorded testimonies are accepted by chamber.
The testimonies of P-0008 and P-1164 cover the extrajudicial killings allegedly perpetrated by police in the context of the drug war, including specific incidents included.
Meanwhile, P-1303’s testimony – in addition to covering some specific incidents – also includes general evidence on matters related to drug use.

articles.title: Poll: Only 28% see fair ruling in VP impeachment
articles.summary: Compared to previous impeachment trials, a smaller proportion of Filipinos expect a fair ruling in the ongoing Senate proceedings against Vice President Sara Duterte, a survey by Social Weather…

blocks.text: Headlines
October 24, 2026 | 12:00am
Vice President Sara Duterte at the 54th Datu Bago Awards Conferment 2026 in Davao City.
Vice President Sara Duterte via Facebok

MANILA, Philippines — Compared to previous impeachment trials, a smaller proportion of Filipinos expect a fair ruling in the ongoing Senate proceedings against Vice President Sara Duterte, a survey by Social Weather Stations (SWS) showed.
The poll, conducted from Sept. 21 to 27, found that only 28 percent of the respondents have “much trust” in the Senate that it would make a fair decision in the impeachment trial.

It was lower than the 32 percent obtained in December 2000 during the impeachment trial of then-president Joseph Estrada and the 30 percent obtained in March 2012 during the trial of then Supreme Court chief justice Renato Corona.
At 35 percent, more Filipinos also have little trust now in the Senate to make a fair decision. It was only at 15 percent in December 2000 and 19 percent in March 2012.
Based on the latest survey, only 42 percent of the respondents closely follow Duterte’s impeachment trial.
Twenty-one percent said they were following it “just a little,” while 27 percent said they were not following at all. Nine percent just heard about the trial from the survey.
Asked about the fairness of proceedings, 50 percent said the Senate impeachment court “has the right consideration for both sides.”

Seventeen percent said the court was too liberal with the prosecutors, while 18 percent said it was too liberal for Duterte’s lawyers. Fifteen percent said they do not know or refused to answer the question.

Only 31 percent said the trial was moving at the right pace, while 39 percent said it was “much too slow.” Twenty-percent thought it was “too much in a hurry,” with the remaining seven percent not providing an answer.
The survey was conducted just as the prosecution wrapped up its presentation of evidence.
The House prosecutors on Oct. 13 formally dropped three out of the four Articles of Impeachment, leaving the issue of unexplained wealth as the sole charge against Duterte.
The court resumes session on Nov. 18, with the defense to begin its presentation of evidence.
Ombudsman studies dropped raps vs VP

Meanwhile, the Office of the Ombudsman will “evaluate” the allegations against Vice President Duterte, including alleged anomalies in her statement of assets, liabilities and net worth (SALN) and the bribery charge already withdrawn from the impeachment trial against her.

Journalists asked Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla about updates on the turnover of Duterte’s SALN records and the possible referral of the withdrawn Articles of Impeachment, including the bribery charge, to the ombudsman during his visit to Cebu last Thursday.

Earlier this month, the House prosecution panel decided to withdraw the three out of four Articles of Impeachment against Duterte including the charge of bribery to officials of the Department of Education that she previously headed. They noted they may refer the bribery charge to the ombudsman or the Department of Justice for possible investigation.
During the media briefing, Remulla said ombudsman investigators “will be needing sworn statements.”
“We will evaluate it first and we will see if we need sworn statements… we cannot take it just on word na walang people standing up to the facts,” he explained.
The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) previously announced it has transferred the case buildup over the alleged misdeclarations in Duterte’s SALN to the ombudsman.
According to Remulla, the NBI’s turnover would undergo fact-finding by his office. – Ghio Ong

articles.title: Oil spill washes up on UAE beaches after tanker strike
articles.summary: Satellite images show oil spreading for miles along the coastline, threatening local marine wildlife
articles.byline: Thomas Copeland, Mark Poynting and Tom Spencer

blocks.text: ByThomas Copeland, Mark Poynting and Tom Spencer
BBC Verify
An oil spill from a tanker attacked near the Strait of Hormuz is spreading along the United Arab Emirates (UAE) coastline, forcing the closure of some beaches and coastal areas.

Satellite images from Monday show the beginnings of the oil spill from a ship matching the location and dimensions of Gem No.2, which was damaged between 9 and 10 October during a record surge of vessel strikes by Iran.
The slick of oil had spread more than 35km (22 miles) from the tanker by Wednesday, the satellite imagery showed.
UAE authorities said on Thursday that the incident is affecting beaches near the northern city of Umm Al Quwain and verified video from Friday shows the oil washing ashore, colouring the water black.

blocks.caption: Side-by-side images of the same beach in the northern UAE. The left image, labelled February 2026, shows clear turquoise water washing onto a clean sandy shoreline. The right image, labelled October 2026, shows a dark band of oil contamination along the waterline, with blackened patches visible w…

blocks.text: The UAE's Ministry of Climate Change and Environment said on Thursday that it "immediately began containment" in order to "limit environmental impacts".

Prof Steve Widdicombe, director of Sharjah Marine Science Research Centre in the UAE, told BBC Verify it was "inevitable that there will be an impact", but researchers caution it is too soon to assess extent of the damage.
Initially a much smaller oil leak could be seen emerging from the ship on 19 October.

blocks.caption: Side-by-side satellite images of a tanker at sea on 19 October. The left image, in colour, shows a dark plume trailing from the vessel and spreading into a curved slick behind it. The right radar image shows the same tanker with a long curved trail extending from its stern, indicating a leak afte…

blocks.text: But the slick appears to have rapidly spread over two days, according to radar satellite imagery reviewed by BBC Verify and intelligence firm MAIAR.

blocks.caption: Satellite image of the Gulf near the UAE coast showing a dark oil slick stretching from a leaking tanker. Annotations indicate the slick was about 35 kilometres long on 21 October. An inset map locates the incident near the Strait of Hormuz between Iran and the UAE. Source: Copernicus Sentinel-1.

blocks.text: Oil spills can cause immediate deaths of marine animals and other organisms, for example by physically trapping turtles, smothering the feathers of seabirds or damaging the gills of fish.
They can also cause longer-lasting damage, Prof Widdicombe said, if species remain exposed to toxic compounds from the oil which could impact their ability to reproduce.

Researchers have cautioned the environmental impact at this stage is very uncertain, as it depends on factors including the volume and type of oil spilled, how quickly it evaporates or breaks down and the effectiveness of the clean-up operation.

But the spill does extend towards Siniyah and Khor Al Beidah islands, a globally recognised Key Biodiversity Area containing habitats like corals, seagrasses and saltmarshes, as well as species including green turtles and the critically endangered Halavi guitarfish.
The proximity of the spill to this area is the "most concerning environmental angle", according to Eoghan Darbyshire, a scientist at the Conflict and Environment Observatory.
Tanker hit 14 days ago
BBC Verify analysis of the dimensions and location of the ship indicate they match a crude oil tanker called Gem No.2.

Maritime intelligence firm Vanguard reported the Panama-flagged tanker was "struck by an unknown projectile" on 9 October, just north of the town of Al Jazeera Al Hamra, causing a fire on board that was later extinguished.
Verified footage first posted on social media on 10 October showed the crew running across the deck and putting on lifejackets as a large cloud of black smoke rose over the ship.

blocks.caption: Three images from a ship at sea showing smoke rising on the horizon. In the left image, thick dark smoke billows into the night sky beside a vessel's deck. In the centre image, crew members wearing safety gear stand on a ship's deck as smoke rises in the distance. In the right image, a large plum…

blocks.text: Iranian state media shared footage of a ship matching Gem No.2 which appeared to show the vessel on fire with burning oil spilling into the sea.
The ship had been attempting to exit the Strait of Hormuz via an "unauthorized and dangerous route", according to state media.
All 22 Indian crew members were rescued, the Indian consulate in Dubai said on 11 October.
Gem No.2 is one of a record number of ships that reported being attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz at the start of October.

Security experts told BBC Verify this was part of an Iranian effort to assert greater control over the strait, in response to the US military successfully escorting more vessels through the vital shipping lane.
Tankers and other commercial vessels have come under attack from both Iranian and US forces in and around the Strait of Hormuz amid the conflict between the two countries.
Another major oil slick washed up on the shores of Iran's Qeshm Island in August, which experts said threatened wildlife, protected ecosystems and fishing communities.
Additional reporting by Charlotte Green

articles.title: Jordan: Karak church shooting leaves 7 dead, dozens injured
articles.summary: A shooting at a Greek Orthodox church in southern Jordan happened during a funeral, according to local authorities. Two unidentified men opened fire on the procession.

image.caption: Jordanian state media published surveillance video of the attack in the village of Hammoud in Karak Governorate Image: Al Mamlaka TV/AFP

blocks.text: A shooting at a church in the southern Jordanian governorate of Karak left seven people dead and another 34 wounded on Friday, Jordan's public security director Obaidallah Maaytah said.
What do we know so far?
The shooting occurred at the Hammoud Church. The shooting reportedly occurred during a funeral.
The attackers' identities and motives remain unclear. Two men opened fire on the funeral procession.

A witness told Jordanian state media there were 150 to 200 people present at the church at the time of the shooting. Videos circulating online showed wounded people on the floor of the church covered in blood, but this footage cannot be verified by DW.

Jordan's Interior Minister Mazen Al-Faraya said a group of "extremists" carried out the massacre. According to Jordanian outlet Roya News, Al-Faraya said authorities already possess the names of suspects behind the attacks but they will not publicly disclose the identities as of now.
Jordanian government spokesperson Mohammad al-Momani said security forces have launched a probe into the attack.
Jordan King Abdullah II: 'We will strike with an iron fist'
Jordan King Abdullah II said "the terrorist attack against Karak will be met with the harshest retaliation."

"Those who delude themselves into thinking that they can divide Jordanians with their bullets have no chance in the face of our unity," Abdullah II said, adding, "We will strike with an iron fist against those who dare to threaten our nation."
Lebanese President Joseph Aoun, a Christian, also condemned the "heinous terrorist attack" in Jordan and expressed condolences to the victims.
US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz said the news regarding the attack is "devastating."

"Praying for the victims, their families and all those affected by this depraved and brutal attack on a house of worship," Waltz said. "Attacks on Christians continue to escalate worldwide and must be stopped."
Gun attacks like the one on the church in Karak are rare in Jordan.

Although Jordan is largely a Muslim-majority country of around 11.5 million people, there is a small Christian minority of a couple hundred thousand. The Karak region, about 180 kilometers (110 miles) south of Amman, has a significant Christian population.
Middle East conflicts take toll on Jordan's tourism sector

articles.title: Undas 2026: Bus terminals see early passenger surge for holiday exodus
articles.summary: Several passengers have started traveling to the provinces more than a week ahead of Undas, filling bus terminals early either to beat the holiday rush or to secure their tickets before the surge of…

blocks.text: Published October 23, 2026 11:20pm

Several passengers have started traveling to the provinces more than a week ahead of Undas, filling bus terminals early either to beat the holiday rush or to secure their tickets before the surge of crowds.

In a “24 Oras” report by Marisol Abdurahman on Friday, security at the Parañaque Integrated Terminal Exchange (PITX) was noticeably tighter, with baggage required to undergo inspection and scanning, while K-9 units were also deployed to check some bags.

The PITX expects passenger volume to reach up to 1.8 million from October 25 to November 4, but noted that some commuters might schedule their trips with the long weekend for the ASEAN Summit from November 16 to 18.

Several passengers queued at ticketing booths—some were buying tickets on-site, others who booked online were retrieving their boarding passes, while some found that tickets to their destinations had already sold out.
Precila Macatangay, a passenger, went to PITX early hoping to travel to Bicol immediately. However, she was only able to secure a 9 p.m. trip.
“Wala nang available. Mas maganda sana earlier para kunyari dating namin dun para umaga safe kami sa pag-uwi sa kaniya-kaniyang baloy,” Macatangay said.
(No earlier trips were available. It would have been better to leave earlier so we could arrive in the morning and safely head to our respective homes.)
Some passengers also went directly to the terminal to purchase tickets after seeing that the next available trips online were already scheduled for Sunday.
According to PITX, certain routes really fill up quickly, but they are assured that there will be enough trips for the Undas exodus.
“Makakasakay at makakasakay pa rin sila dito sa PITX dahil marami naman tayong nakaabang na additional units,” PITX spokesperson Jason Salvador said.
(They will definitely be able to get a ride here at PITX because we have plenty of additional bus units standing by.)
At the Araneta Bus Port in Cubao, Quezon City, the situation remains quiet, although some travelers have also opted to head to the provinces early for Undas.
A passenger shared that while they usually travel to their province in their private vehicle, they chose to commute this year due to high fuel prices.
“Sayang naman ‘yung gas, mas mahal sobrang mahal… Para makatipid, sakto lalo't may inaasahan na namang tataas ang presyo ng diesel sa susunod na linggo,” said Merlee Mendoza, a passenger.
(Gasoline is too expensive now... To save money, commuting makes sense, especially with another diesel price hike expected next week.)
The Araneta City Bus Port management stated that they are also expecting an influx of province-bound passengers in the coming days.
“We will be expecting ng karagdagan ding ruta. May ini-expect kaming isang operator papasok to Bicol,” Araneta City Bus Port Manager Ramon Legazpi said.
(We are expecting additional routes. We expect one operator to open trips heading to Bicol.) —Lyjah Tiffany Bonzo/LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Afghan women could lose one of their last paths to a higher education
articles.summary: The US has defunded the last university giving Afghan women the opportunity to receive an education after the Taliban takeover in 2021. DW spoke with a student who says she's lost hope of ever…

image.caption: After the Taliban banned women from attending university, students turned to online classes Image: ALI KHARA/REUTERS

blocks.text: "Laila" awoke in the middle of the night for a glass of water, checked her phone almost by accident, and saw an email that made her stomach drop. The US would stop funding the American University of Afghanistan (AUAF), one of the last places women can still study in the country.
Laila said she sat on her bed, staring, her thoughts racing through the past five years and everything she had endured just to get an education.
It had not been easy to find a way to study in Afghanistan after the Taliban outlawed women's education.

The American University campus was already taken over by the Taliban, but she could study secretly through the university's online program. But now that the university is losing its financing, she told DW she and her classmates fear it will shut down entirely. Her name has been changed for safety reasons.
In Afghanistan, girls study in secret to skirt Taliban ban
A hidden education for women in Afghanistan
Laila is in her mid-twenties. She studies political science and international studies and is one of around 1,000 enrolled students at the university, three-quarters of them women.

When the Taliban returned to power in August 2021, Laila was studying at another university in Kabul, with just two final exams remaining to finish her semester. Then, in December 2022, the Taliban announced the ban. Laila's degree was left unfinished.
Laila secured a scholarship to AUAF and started over. "Not every girl got that opportunity," she said.

Laila has told few people outside of her family about her online studies. On most days, she stays home for remote lectures, alongside classmates who use aliases and keep their cameras off for security. "I just know their voices," she said.

Laila speaks English with an American accent. She learned it as a child, watching cartoons. In her early twenties, she was learning even more about the world outside Afghanistan and studying foreign governments.

Then on August 14, 2021, Laila's life changed. She and a friend sat in a restaurant in Kabul. They had just finished an exam and wanted to celebrate passing the test by ordering coffee and cake. Suddenly, a man came in, stopped at the entrance, and shouted "Allahu Akbar." He yelled that the mujahideen would always be victorious.
That was the day the Taliban retook power in Afghanistan, they soon forced women out of public life, banning them from many jobs and from attending school and university.
Exiled Afghanistan envoy still advocating for women's rights

Laila said she recalls losing feeling in her hands or feet. She pulled money from her purse and slammed it on the table without checking the amount. "We all thought maybe this would be the last day that we are alive," she said.
Since then, some of Laila's peers have received threatening calls and messages. Now, whenever she leaves home, she worries that Taliban authorities might search her phone.
"What if they see my emails from my work, from my university?" she said. "It's always in the back of my head that maybe tomorrow it's my turn. Maybe they will detain me."
Even her home isn't safe. Laila said Taliban authorities have entered on several occasions to search their belongings.
Yet, she has continued studying. For all its limitations and risks, the online program offered a chance to graduate.
A place for Afghanistan's 'future leaders'
With the US pulling out as the university's primary funder, Laila said she doubts whether she has the strength to start over.

The American University of Afghanistan was always intended, largely, for women. Before the campus opened in 2006, former US first lady Laura Bush announced that the US had committed millions to support it.
Appearing in Kabul, Bush said the new university would teach "future leaders," particularly women. Women like Laila, who was four years old at the time.
"These are more than just development projects," Bush said at the time. "They also signify the bond between the American and Afghan people. They are symbols of our shared hopes and dreams."

Patrick Fine was Afghanistan mission director at USAID, the now-defunct American development agency. Fine told DW that many at USAID considered the university idea risky. Critics thought training elites was a waste of money.
But the Bush administration saw an opportunity to stabilize a budding democracy, Fine said.

By 2003, the Taliban had been driven from power. US President George W. Bush wanted to foster goodwill for the US-backed interim government that had replaced the Taliban. The university served that goal, and also offered other "facets of advantage" in educating women, training future politicians, and supporting the Afghan economy.
"It really impacted the lives of thousands of Afghan youth," Fine said, referencing alumni. "The organization has managed to achieve that against incredible odds."
How 5 years of Taliban rule have changed Afghanistan
Washington pulls the plug
The university continued with US support. But in Washington, that support started to come under question.

The US government suspected the university of mishandling money. In 2016, US inspectors opened an investigation into its finances. By 2018, investigators said they could not tell exactly how it was spending US aid money, because its accounting was so poor.
John Sopko, a former US federal inspector, oversaw that investigation. When DW contacted him for this story, he replied, "I was surprised they were still funding AUAF."

This year, after the funding was pulled, the US State Department Press Office told DW in an email that the move was made given the university's "history of repeated lack of accountability for millions of American taxpayer dollars."
Fine, the former USAID director, rejected the State Department's fraud explanation.
"Those are just smear tactics," he said. He conceded that past audits found the university struggling to keep up with USAID's extensive rules, "but they didn't find major fraud," he said.
"It is still a useful investment, a worthy investment," Fine said, "and the reason for that is that it's one of the few organizations left that is reaching Afghan women."
The US isn't the university's only funder, but it has long covered most of its costs: nearly 90% as of 2018, according to a US report.

The US State Department told DW that the university is "free to identify other funders and partners, so the end of their receipt of American taxpayer money does not necessarily equate to an end to their operations."
But without the $25 million grant the State Department recently refused, the university's future is in doubt.
What is next for women students in Afghanistan?
"I have lost all my motivation and hope," Laila said, adding that each time she prepares for a lecture, she wonders whether there will be another.

Since she learned about the funding cut, she said she's barely left her room. Her curtains are usually closed, and she's lost her appetite. "Maybe I'm so disappointed that I can't even cry about it," she said.

She said she was supposed to have graduated years ago. She was supposed to be making the world a better place. She was supposed to be in studying a master's degree abroad. Now, she's thinking, maybe she'll find a way in five or ten years.
Afghan female artists in exile showcase their culture

articles.title: EXPLAINER: What is the Shamonda virus?
articles.summary: France recently reported its first case of the Shamonda virus, with the patient reportedly dying; authorities are still determining if the virus caused the death. But what is the Shamonda virus?

blocks.text: Published October 23, 2026 10:52pm
France recently reported its first case of the Shamonda virus, with the patient reportedly dying; authorities are still determining if the virus caused the death.
But what is the Shamonda virus?
According to GMA News Feed, the first case of the Shamonda virus infecting a human was reported in France on October 22.

According to the European Center for Disease Prevention and Control, the patient died earlier in October while being treated for a “serious illness,” which made the patient more vulnerable to the virus.
French authorities suspect that the patient was bitten by a midge that carried the virus in the eastern part of the country.

The World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH) said that the Shamonda virus reportedly affected cattle more often, but there have also been cases where sheep, goats, horses and alpacas were infected.
The Shamonda virus is vector-borne and is transmitted through midge bites.

While there is currently no evidence of animal-to-animal transmission of the virus, WOAH says that vertical transmission, or transmission from a parent to the embryo, fetus or newborn, has been reported.
The Shamonda virus belongs to the Simbu serogroup. Other members of the group include the Schmallenberg virus, a virus that can cause reproductive disorders in livestock.
It was first identified in Nigerian cattle in 1965, according to the WOAH. Since then, the virus has also been reported in other regions of Africa and Asia.
European cases of the virus were first identified in July 2026.

Signs of the Shamonda virus in animals include fever, diarrhea, reduced milk production, reproductive disorders such as abortions and fetal malformation. Less commonly, there can be neurological disorders, which have been reported in horses.
The WOAH said that the Shamonda virus has not infected humans historically,
The World Health Organization said that the case in France is likely isolated and is unlikely to spread.

“The general public, fit, well people, have very little to worry about from Shamonda. It's primarily an animal pathogen… The disease is fairly consequential in the animals that get infected and will cause economic problems for any farmer or farms, etc., that are affected by the virus. But human populations certainly, at the moment, from everything we know, have very little to worry about,” said Senior Lecturer in Virology Ben Brennan of Glasgow University said. —Jean Mangaluz/LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Melania Trump brokers truce for Ukraine city 'on brink of disaster', White House says
articles.summary: Ukraine and Russia have not confirmed the truce in Russian-occupied Oleshky, where residents have had to eat garden weeds to survive.

blocks.text: US First Lady Melania Trump has "successfully secured" a ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky, the White House has said.
The statement said the truce in the "front-line war city on the brink of disaster" would begin on 29 October, though Ukraine and Russia have so far not commented.
"Oleshky's remaining population is comprised primarily of elderly residents who urgently need medical attention, medicine, food, and clean water," it added.

Oleshky, in the Kherson region, was seized by Russian forces during the first days of Moscow's full-scale invasion in February 2022. Remaining residents have recently resorted to eating garden weeds to survive.
The White House statement said Melania Trump and her representative had worked "directly with Russian and Ukrainian leadership to define the terms of the localised ceasefire".
"Non-military, civilian leaders from both countries will work together to visit Oleshky residents in their homes and determine the level of assistance they require," she is quoted as saying.
"Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine."

Melania Trump added that Oleshky residents "have limited electricity, live amid mined roads, and endure regular military attacks" and that "without my intervention, the possibility to bring humanitarian aid into the city and to evacuate the elderly would be impossible".
The statement did not say how long the ceasefire would be in place for.
Last month, some of the remaining Oleshky residents told the BBC harrowing accounts of how they were surviving in the city that was being constantly shelled and cut off from food and water.
They said that children remaining in wider Oleshky were suffering from malnutrition, a lack of medical services and were "degrading" without access to education.
Many also told the BBC there was only one hospital partially operational, opening a few days a week to perform critical amputations.
The local population was living under a "full blockade" by Russian forces, according to Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha.
Ukraine says it has attempted to deliver supplies to the area but has not had success in recent months.

The Kremlin in September acknowledged that Oleshky was facing "a critical situation" and "problems with supplies of food and medicine", but added that "Russia's military was working to resolve them" and blamed Kyiv.
Occupied by Russia since 2022, Oleshky is trapped between the Dnipro River, which separates it from Ukrainian positions, and Russian forces.

articles.title: Romania blames Russia for ship attack in the Black Sea
articles.summary: Russian strikes against ships attempting to export Ukrainian grain and cargo through the western Black Sea have sharply increased this month.

image.caption: Romanian president blames Russia for the ship attack in western Black Sea [FILE: May 2026]Image: Malina Norocea/Inquam Photos/REUTERS

blocks.text: Romanian President Nicusor Dan blamed Russia for an attack on a merchant vessel in the Black Sea on Friday morning.
A drone strike sank the merchant ship, with 13 Ukrainian and Azeri crew members on board, near Romanian territorial waters.
The attack killed at least 1 sailor, and three others were still missing, according to Dan.
Nine of the 13 crew members have been rescued.
Attack on merchant shipping on the rise in the Black Sea: What to know
The drone strike on the ship, called Khoryv, is believed to be the fourth merchant vessel to have been attacked off the coast of Romania this month.
Two weeks ago, two merchant vessels were also set ablaze in the western Black Sea, which is a vital shipping corridor heavily used by Ukraine.
One of those ships was inside Romanian territorial waters. Romania raised concerns about Russian provocation in waters at the edge of or controlled by NATO members.
That's because Bulgaria, also a NATO member like Romania, has raised similar concerns too.
Bulgaria has raised concerns about Russian strikes having edged too close to its exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea after merchant ships were hit by drones earlier this month too.
Both Romania and Bulgaria have blamed Russia for the attacks and have called on the alliance to do more to protect commercial shipping in the Black Sea.
NATO said earlier this week that it was sending more maritime patrol aircraft and radar systems to the Black Sea without having blamed any country for the attacks there.
About 23 sailors had been reported dead or missing in incidents in the Black Sea in the 10 days leading up to October 15, according to Reuters.
That tally is higher now.

Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, condemned the increasing attacks on vessels in the Black Sea too, earlier this month calling it "unacceptable" that "the Black Sea has become another front of escalation of the Russian war in Ukraine."
How Russian aggression is shaping Bulgaria's presidential election

articles.title: Ukraine tries to shut Moscow's airports with drone strikes on Russia
articles.summary: Repeated Ukrainian drone attacks are increasingly disrupting operations at Moscow's airports. The pounding is part of Ukraine's plan to shut down Russia's airpace.

image.caption: Passengers wait in line at Moscow's Sheremetyevo International AirportImage: Alexey Belkin/Russian Look/news.ru/press.media/picture alliance

blocks.text: For months, drone strikes by Ukraine have forced the suspension of flights to and from airports in Russia. Moscow's Domodedovo, Sheremetyevo, Zhukovsky and Vnukovo airports have had to shut down operations almost daily in October, according to reports from the independent investigative media outlet Agentstvo. On some days, the airports were reportedly closed for up to nine hours.

In early September, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced that Ukraine would seek to cut off the airspace around Moscow and other destinations in Russia. "Today, we would like to warn every airline that uses Russian airspace, every insurer, and everyone who continues to use major Russian airports: Russian airspace will become completely unsafe," Zelenskyy said.
The following day, Ukraine sent a corresponding warning to the International Civil Aviation Organization.
Ukraine's airspace has been closed since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Poland's ex-president: Putin's war in Ukraine was a miscalculation
Can Ukraine succeed?

Russia's aviation authority, Rosaviatsiya, has issued an emergency safety "carpet" protocol that is designed to immediately shut down the airspace over a specific region or around affected airports if an aircraft violates Russian airspace, weapons are used, or unidentified objects appear in the skies. Once the protocol is announced, drastic restrictions apply to all air traffic.

"If there is a military threat, a specific section of airspace is closed off, and this carpet is declared," Oleksandr Laneckij, the chief executive officer of the Friendly Avia Support consultancy, told DW. "Essentially, every drone poses a military threat."
Laneckij noted that Yemen's Houthis have managed to significantly disrupt Saudi airspace. "I think Ukraine's military capabilities far exceed those of the Houthis," Laneckij said.

blocks.caption: Sheremetyevo International Airport is the busiest in MoscowImage: Valery Sharifulin/TASS/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The military analyst Jan Matvejev also said Ukraine would have little trouble severely disrupting Moscow-area air traffic. Though Ukraine has not yet managed to completely shut down Russian airspace as Zelenskyy plans, Matvejev said, its armed forces "remain committed to this idea."

"To close off the airspace and trigger the 'carpet' plan, all you need are simple drones that don't have to be equipped with a warhead or even have a long range," Matvejev said. Ukraine's arms industry can produce hundreds of combat-ready long-range drones in a day, he added. That is why he believes Ukraine could have the necessary resources to shut down Moscow's airports.
Indeed, Ukraine's efforts to shut down Russian airspace are "just getting started," Simon Shuster wrote in October in the US magazine The Atlantic, citing well-informed sources.
Can Russia stop Ukraine's drones?

Matvejev said Russia's air-defense systems were not entirely effective in efforts to prevent Ukrainian drones from penetrating Moscow's airspace. "If it were possible to shoot them down, they would have done so by now," he said. He added that Russia would have deployed additional air-defense troops if they were available.

Laneckij said Russia might lower the threshold for declaring the carpet protocol, which could increase the risk of deadly incidents such as the 2024 Christmas day crash of an Azerbaijan Airlines flight. Investigators say the flight was struck by a Russian air-defense missile that was being used to defend against drones, killing 38 people.

Matvejev seconded the fear that Russia's defenses could again mistakenly target civilian aircraft instead of military objects. He said little had changed about Russia's air-defense protocol since the Azeri flight was shot in 2024.

In an operation against a low-flying drone, the target is visually identified and fired upon with a machine gun. In such a scenario, the danger to aircraft is extremely low, unless they happen to be flying in the immediate vicinity.

The risk to civil aviation increases significantly when anti-aircraft missiles are deployed, Matvejev said. A missile could have defects that are practically unavoidable in mass production and could veer toward an aircraft flying nearby. Matvejev said such defense measures could not guarantee the safety of civilian aircraft during operations.

blocks.caption: The site of the Azerbaijan Airlines plane shot down by a Russian missileImage: Meiramgul Kussainova/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: He said drones did not have to carry explosives to be disruptive. A collision between an airplane and a basic drone can have serious consequences — and, he said, a drone sent from Ukraine all the way to Moscow must be relatively large, "weighting dozens of kilograms."

In the summer of 2023, Ukrainian armed forces attacked the airport in the Russian city of Pskov, where both military and civilian aircraft were parked. Earlier this month, drone debris fell on the Sochi airport, on Russia's Black Sea coast.
Russia also attacks Ukraine's airports. In September, Zelenskyy said Kyiv's airport had been struck, as well as the Boryspil airport near the capital.
How will international airlines react?
Laneckij said three factors would determine whether international airlines suspend their flights to Russia: the military threat, the degree of demand and the insurance cost.

He said issues could emerge around insurance. When insurers rate the security risk of flying to Russia as very high, they could significantly raise their rates for aircraft headed there. This would cause ticket prices to skyrocket.

Competition within Russia's aviation market has already declined because many airlines are no longer in business, Laneckij said. This has increased demand for tickets from the remaining foreign airlines.
"Whether they stay or not depends on the price they have to pay for the danger faced," he said.
This article was translated from German.

articles.title: Motorcycle taxi riders urge LTFRB not to drop riders due to over-boarding
articles.summary: Some motorcycle taxi rider groups have staged a protest in front of the Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board (LTFRB) office on Monday, urging the agency not to drop riders over issues…

blocks.text: Published October 23, 2026 10:12pm

Some motorcycle taxi rider groups have staged a protest in front of the Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board (LTFRB) office on Monday, urging the agency not to drop riders over issues of "overboarding" and "ghost riders."
In a “24 Oras” report by Jonathan Andal, overboarding refers to a situation where the number of riders on a ride-hailing application or platform exceeds the limit set by the government.

According to Jayson Luna, co-convenor of the Motorcycle Riders Association (METRO), there is a cap of only 15,000 riders per platform, and as of now, the number of active riders on some platforms appears to have already exceeded that limit.
“Ito po ‘yung mga kasamahan namin na hindi alam na napaloob doon sa iba't ibang platform na platform provider. Hindi namin alam kung kami kasama roon sa labis na itinalaga ng gobyerno,” Luna said.
(These are our fellow riders who didn't know they were included in those different platform providers. We don't know if we are among those in excess of the limit set by the government.)
He added that they fear riders exceeding the LTFRB-set limit might be banned from operating.
Meanwhile, the riders' group KAGULONG argued that overboarding is not the riders’ fault, as it was the ride-hailing apps that accepted their applications to become MC taxi riders.

“Ang usapan with the LTFRB ay walang mawawalan ng trabaho, walang maiiwang rider… ‘Yung issue ng overboarding, hindi kasalanan ng rider ‘yan… Kaya hindi dapat ang rider ang mag-suffer dun sa nangyayaring mga kalokohan na ‘yan,” KAGULONG Secretary General Don Pangan said.

(The understanding with the LTFRB was that no one would lose their job, and no rider would be left behind... The issue of overboarding is not the riders' fault... So the riders should not suffer from the irregularities taking place.)
Following the rally, Pangan and Luna were called inside the LTFRB office, where they spoke with the agency's executive director.
In a text message, LTFRB Acting Chairman Greg Pua stated he was in Tacloban at the time.
According to Luna, the LTFRB official assured them that no MC rider would lose their job once the institutionalization process for MC taxi riders moves forward.
At present, riders are awaiting the passage of the law that will formally recognize MC taxis as public utility vehicles.
GMA News is trying to obtain a statement from the LTFRB regarding the matter and will publish it once available. –Lyjah Tiffany Bonzo/NB, GMA News

articles.title: Many feared trapped under collapsed building in Nairobi
articles.summary: People are feared to be trapped after a large, unfinished building in Nairobi collapsed during construction. Rescue operations have proven complicated as police fired tear gas to disperse looters.

image.caption: Building collapses and constructions are unfortunately not uncommon in Nairobi, KenyaImage: Brian Inganga/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: A multi-story building that was still under construction collapsed in the Kenyan capital of Nairobi on Friday, resulting in casualties and looting at the site, according to local media.
The Nairobi County governor's ​office confirmed the collapse, adding in a ​statement that people may be trapped beneath rubble.
Videos spreading online showed a dramatic crash and huge clouds of dust as the building came down in a busy business-residential mixed-use district.
The Red Cross sent teams to the site, posting on social media: "At around 1340 hours, a multi-story building under construction collapsed on 9th Street in Eastleigh, Nairobi."

There were conflicting reports on the size of the unfinished building. Nairobi Police Chief Issa Mohamud said the building had more than 10 floors under construction, while other accounts range from 12 to 18 stories.
Governor Johnson Sakaja's ​office said only the building's ground floor ​was occupied.

"There were some businesses in the basement, and workers who were busy building," local resident Abdi Aziz, 25, told the AFP news agency. "But since it was Friday prayers, a lot of them were at the mosque."
Rescue work underway at Nairobi building collapse site
A video published by Reuters news agency showed people gathered at the scene as ⁠an excavator moved rubble.

But rescue operations were proving complicated. Police officers sought to clear the area and provide access to emergency response teams but had to fire tear gas at people who had begun looting neighboring shops.
Eastleigh is a densely packed residential and market area, known as a hub for the Somali community.

It was not ​clear what caused the building to collapse. Nairobi is undergoing an extremely rapid construction boom, with high-rise buildings shooting up all over the city as Kenya's population expands.

blocks.caption: Rescue work was underway in Nairobi, with some people feared trappedImage: Brian Inganga/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Kenya: How common are building collapses?
Building collapses are a recurring problem in Nairobi.
County officials responsible for issuing building permits have been accused of failing to conduct adequate inspections to ensure developers comply with construction standards and safety guidelines.
There were 86 building collapses between 2009 and 2019, killing an estimated 200 people, according to a report by the Kenya Institute for Public Policy Research and Analysis.
Meanwhile, a separate audit of almost 15,000 buildings by the National Building Inspectorate found that 4.8% were very dangerous while 72.3% were classified as unsafe.

articles.title: Ebola patient in Nigeria did not visit DR Congo, escalating concern over spread of virus
articles.summary:
Switzerland says patient is wife of Swiss diplomat and believed to have contracted virus while travelling in Uganda

An Ebola patient in Nigeria is a Swiss woman who has not travelled to the…
articles.byline: Carlos Mureithi in Nairobi and agencies

blocks.text: Health officials across Africa are racing to determine how Nigeria’s first Ebola patient ⁠in more than a decade ⁠became infected, amid fears ​the outbreak could spread further after reaching a fourth African country.

The Swiss foreign ministry said on Friday the patient in Nigeria, the Ugandan-born wife of a Swiss diplomat based in Abuja, had not travelled to the Democratic Republic of ⁠Congo, where the outbreak was first detected in mid-May before spreading to Uganda, Kenya and now Nigeria. The woman was believed to have contracted Ebola while travelling with her husband in Uganda, the ministry added.

The new information contradicts accounts from Uganda, which previously said the woman had travelled to eastern DR Congo, and will raise concerns about the ability of authorities to contain the outbreak, which is already the most geographically widespread in history.

The Ugandan government reported Ebola cases in May and June before WHO declared it Ebola-free in August. A Ugandan government spokesperson told Reuters on Thursday that Uganda had no ​Ebola cases and that, if ​it did, it would make that information ​public.
The World Health Organization said investigations were continuing to establish the likely source of infection for the Ebola patient in Nigeria.

The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention is investigating whether the patient may have come into contact with an Ebola patient in Kenya, as both travelled from Uganda’s Entebbe airport on 3 October, said Dr Wessam Mankoula, head of emergency preparedness and response at the organisation.

Catherine Smallwood, a WHO Ebola incident manager in DR Congo, told a UN briefing in Geneva via video ‌link on Friday that WHO staff in DR Congo had no information showing the patient in Nigeria had travelled to the country.

Smallwood said a link to the case in Kenya was possible, ​but added that officials would need to compare the timing with when the Nigeria patient’s symptoms began to tell whether the infection more likely happened at the Ugandan airport or elsewhere.

Marion Koopmans, a Dutch virologist and member of the WHO’s Ebola emergency committee, cast doubt on the theory. “I think that is very speculative unless there is evidence of sharing the same ​space in a manner that could explain that,” she said. “Random presence at the same location, a large airport, is not a supported epidemiological link by any standard of what we currently know.”

The Nigerian health minister, Muhammad Ali Pate, said Nigeria’s case remains contained and that contact-tracing was continuing. “We are trying to contain it so it doesn’t go out to the communities. Hopefully, it won’t get to that and we are working hard to ensure that,” Pate said.

Melaku Yirga, vice-president for Africa at Prosper Global (formerly Mercy Corps), said the confirmation of Ebola in Kenya and Nigeria reinforces the need for countries to work closely together to prevent further transmission.
“What matters most now is speed, sharing information across borders without delay and ensuring frontline health workers and local organiaations have the resources to respond quickly,” he said.

Ebola is a highly contagious and often fatal viral disease that affects humans and non-human primates. It spreads through body fluids or contaminated materials and causes organ damage, blood vessel impairment and sometimes severe internal and external bleeding.

The current outbreak is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has no approved treatment or vaccine. It was first announced on 15 May and has infected more than 9,500 people and killed nearly half of them.

The outbreak is the largest and deadliest in DR Congo’s history and second only ​globally to ​the 2014-16 outbreak in west Africa, which infected ​more than ‌28,600 people ​and ​killed more than 11,000.
Reuters and the Associated Press contributed reporting

articles.title: Seven shot dead by gunmen at church funeral in Jordan, state media say
articles.summary: Another 10 people are injured in the southern Karak governorate, and a manhunt is now under way.

blocks.text: At least seven people were killed when two gunmen opened fire on a funeral in central Jordan, the country's state media report.
Another 10 people were injured in the church in the Karak governorate on Friday.
The unidentified gunmen are reported to have arrived in a car and began shooting inside the church before fleeing the scene.
Security forces have been deployed, government spokesman Mohammad al-Momani said.
Dozens of people had been inside the church for the funeral when the shooting began, Khaled Burqan, one of the mourners, told Jordan's al-Mamlaka state-run TV.
He said the two attackers armed with a rifle and a pistol had been firing at the mourners for several minutes.
No-one has so far claimed responsibility for the attack.

articles.title: Netanyahu orders ‘very extensive’ operation in West Bank after two Israeli soldiers killed
articles.summary:
Israel’s prime minister gives order after military says it thwarted ‘terror attack’ by two armed Palestinians

Benjamin Netanyahu has ordered the army to prepare for a “very extensive”…

blocks.text: Benjamin Netanyahu has ordered the army to prepare for a “very extensive” operation in the occupied West Bank after two Israeli soldiers and two Palestinians were killed in an exchange of fire near a checkpoint in Hebron.

Netanyahu said the military would go house to house and demolish homes in an operation on a scale unseen in the occupied West Bank for decades, after the Israeli military said it had thwarted a “terror attack” by two armed Palestinians on Friday, amid heightened tensions before next week’s election.

According to the Israel Defense Forces, the two assailants opened fire on soldiers at a temporary checkpoint outside Hebron after failing to reach a nearby highway, where the Israeli military believes they had intended to attack civilians. According to a preliminary military investigation, the ensuing gunfight lasted more than 20 minutes, leaving five Israelis wounded, two of whom later succumbed to their injuries.
An AFP photographer who was en route to another assignment and witnessed the gun battle saw two Palestinian men armed with a handgun and an automatic rifle exchanging fire with Israeli forces.
Netanyahu’s office later said it had instructed security forces to immediately cordon off Hebron and prepare for a full closure of the West Bank starting on Friday.

After the shooting, the Israeli prime minister held an emergency meeting of his security cabinet and officials from top military and security agencies. He said Hamas was “planning a major attack aimed at murdering innocent civilians”.

During a visit to Hebron after the attack, Netanyahu later said Israeli forces would enter the neighbourhood of the attackers and displace its residents. He said the military would apply a model previously used in refugee camps in the northern West Bank.
A large-scale military operation named the “Iron Wall” launched in January 2025, forcibly displaced tens of thousands of people across several refugee camps, according to the UN rights office.

“We will evacuate the residents, we will go from house to house, we will also seize the weapons there, and all the terrorist infrastructure will be dealt with and destroyed,” Netanyahu said, according to his office.

Closures of the West Bank are becoming more common. Friday’s lockdown was the fourth time in the past month that Israel had imposed restrictions across the territory, shutting gates and checkpoints connecting Palestinian villages to major roads, which will remain open to Israeli drivers, including settlers, who can still travel through the area.
Bezalel Smotrich, the far-right Israeli finance minister who also holds a position within the defence ministry, called for a military campaign in the West Bank “exactly like in Gaza”.
He said: “There is no other option but a comprehensive military campaign to dismantle the Palestinian Authority, collect weapons and eliminate terrorists. Exactly like in Gaza and Lebanon.”
Smotrich added: “In the next government this will be one of the first measures that we must demand and apply.”

Human rights groups warned that Netanyahu and his government could use the attack on Israeli soldiers to justify tougher measures against Palestinians and bolster their security credentials before the election.

“Every day in the West Bank is a dramatic day for the Palestinians,” Yariv Oppenheimer, the former director of Peace Now told Al Jazeera. “The Israeli army is getting into the Palestinian cities, the settlers are attacking Palestinians, and the situation is impossible.

“There will be house demolitions. We will see [a] curfew. We will see more soldiers … making arrests, and definitely we might see the settlers trying to target Palestinians in revenge for this attack, and trying to take advantage of this situation in order to escalate the situation even more.”

Voters go to the polls on Tuesday in an election that will help to determine whether Netanyahu secures another term as prime minister. The vote comes three years after the Hamas-led attacks on Israel that triggered the war in Gaza.
Israeli settlers are increasingly taking over Palestinian properties, and authorities have stepped up demolitions of homes lacking building permits, displacing families.

The campaign has intensified since the war in Gaza started in October 2023 amid accelerating land seizures and settlement expansion across the occupied West Bank. More than 1,100 Palestinians have been killed there by Israeli forces or settlers, whose violence has surged during the annual olive harvest.

On 16 October settlers attacked Palestinian villages, burning cars and trees and injuring a Washington Post photographer. The next day they attacked European diplomats, a French mayor and Palestinian olive pickers, injuring three people and damaging a diplomatic vehicle.

articles.title: Japan-Russia ties erode as journalist sits in Moscow jail
articles.summary: Japan is demanding access to a journalist who was arrested by Russian security services. Moscow claims Tokyo is using journalists as spies.

image.caption: Journalist Yuki Imai seen being taken into custody by Russian security agents Image: Russian Federal Security Service/TASS/picture alliance

blocks.text: Japanese Foreign Ministry officials were in Moscow this week in an attempt to contact a journalist arrested in Russia's far east on spying claims.

Journalist Yuki Imai was arrested on October 14 by Russia's FSB security service in the city of Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk on Sakhalin Island. Televised footage of the arrest showed FSB officers barging into his hotel room as he slept.

The correspondent for the Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper was accused of attempting to obtain information on soldiers in the region, which is near the Kiril islands, a geopolitical sore spot in Russia-Japan relations.

Russian authorities quickly transferred him to Lefortovo Prison in Moscow, where a court ordered him to be held in pre-trial detention until at least December 12. If convicted, 34-year-old Imai faces up to 20 years in jail, according to the International Federation of Journalists, which has called for his immediate release.
Officials of the Japanese embassy in Moscow have been refused access to Imai. In Tokyo, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has condemned the arrest and dismissed the claim that Imai was a spy.

Russian Ambassador Nikolay Nozdrev said Imai had been caught "red-handed," Russia's TASS news agency reported. He has claimed that Japanese intelligence agencies use Japanese journalists to collect classified information with the goal of "undermining Russia's security and defense capability."
Russia accuses journalists of being 'spies'

Yoji Gomi, a veteran journalist and author who has reported from across Asia, told DW Japanese journalists may occasionally meet with diplomats in the course of their work and "share thoughts and impressions." However, he rejects the idea that reporters are paid spies.
"One-party nations often see foreign correspondents as spies because that is exactly what they use their journalists for," he said.

"I can completely see how the Russians decided that Imai was a spy, as it is how they operate, plus he was in a sensitive part of Russia where there are lots of North Korean laborers that they want to keep quiet," Gomi added.
Japan condemns Putin visit to disputed Kuril Islands

Stephen Nagy, a professor of international relations at Tokyo's International Christian University, said that Russia may see Imai as a bargaining chip it can use to exchange for its nationals detained overseas.
However, Nagy doubts Japan will give in to pressure.

"They are going to resist because it means that Russia, or any other country, can then just seize a Japanese national, put them on trial for espionage and demand the release of one of their people," he told DW.
"It would set a dangerous precedent," he added.
The arrest comes after a member of a Russia-linked hacking group "Qilin" was arrested in Japan and extradited to Germany to face charges in connection with a 2024 cyberattack on a logistics center.

The last time a journalist was arrested in Russia was in 2019 for "attempting to obtain classified information about Russia's military potential in the Far East," Russia's Interfax news agency reported. However, in this case, the journalist was quickly released.

Imai's case is perhaps the most serious since 2023, when Wall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovich was arrested in Russia and sentenced to 16 years in a penal colony before being released in a prisoner exchange with Western countries in 2024.

blocks.caption: Russia has previously arrested foreign journalists for prisoner exchanges. US reporter Evan Gershkovich is seen here in a Moscow court.Image: Dmitry Serebryakov/AP/picture alliance

blocks.text: Strained Japan-Russia ties
Imai's arrest is the latest in a series of incidents that have sent bilateral relations into a tailspin.

Nagy said Imai's seizure is designed to put pressure on Tokyo. He added this is part of a coordinated approach with China to isolate Japan at a time when the US is preoccupied with domestic issues and the conflict in the Middle East.

"Moscow and Beijing are coordinating to create the image that Japan is not a reformed member of the international community but still the military state of the 1930s and that it poses a threat to stability in the Indo-Pacific region," Nagy said.

"This is all designed to smear Japan's efforts to lead diplomacy in the region at a time when the US is perhaps distracted," he told DW. "And it does not even matter much that it is not true; they will just continue to repeat the claim to discredit and weaken Tokyo."
Decades-long row over disputed islands

Tadashi Anno, a professor of politics at Tokyo's Sophia University, believes Japan had been working hard to maintain a stable relationship with Moscow, even after Tokyo joined international condemnation of the invasion of Ukraine.
Anno said Moscow's timing on turning up the heat on Tokyo is puzzling.
"Japan condemned the invasion of Ukraine in 2022 because it was a fundamental violation of international law, but Russia is only now pushing back hard," he told DW.
At the center of deteriorating ties is a territorial dispute about a chain of islands off the far north of Japan that were seized by Soviet forces after Japan's surrender in World War II.

Known as the Northern Territories in Japan and the Southern Kurils by Russia, there have been hopes in the past in Tokyo that a concerted diplomatic effort could be sufficient to convince Russia to return them to Japanese sovereignty.

That campaign has faltered in the last couple of years, however, and was further dented when Japan announced in the spring that it would be joining the NATO initiative to provide non-lethal assistance to Kyiv.

In August, President Vladimir Putin visited the disputed islands, only the second Russian leader to do so. Earlier this month, a delegation of Chinese businesspeople was welcomed on one of the islands and talks are under way on the possibility of economic cooperation.
